utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like the AV booth to play the third excerpt from the tape that we haven't seen until the end yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: In the first half of September 1991, we discussed the need for officers, staff officers, in the Krajina. I asked for this meeting -- in fact, before that, Boro Rasuo and Zoran Kalicanin found a volunteer, a volunteer who would -- who volunteered to go to Krajina, and that was Colonel Radoslav Maksic. And he said that he could find another ten officers for the staff but that the request should be made via Milosevic so that they could meet. And the third point on which I'd like to talk -- "MR. HARDIN: Just a minute. So you said that Rasuo and Kalicanin had found this Radoslav Maksic to come -- "THE INTERPRETER: Maksic, yes. "MR. HARDIN: -- to come to the Krajina, and Maksic said that he could find other officers for the staff. And was it Maksic that said that you needed to take your request to Milosevic? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: Well, we were there -- I was taken to Maksic's apartment, and it was there that we talked about it. "MR. HARDIN: And he was present? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: And as I recollect -- as I recollect, we jointly came to it. Well, I cannot recollect exactly, but we could say it was our common conclusion or position. You see, Maksic was still on active duty as an officer, and he couldn't leave without the approval. And he wanted to have this approval to be able to leave. "MR. HARDIN: So the concurrences that you would go see Milosevic included the concurrences of Maksic, Rasuo, Kalicanin, and yourself? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: Well, as I -- my recollection goes, it was Maksic who insisted that he must have the approval for leaving. That's the way it [inaudible]. "MR. HARDIN: Yes. I understand that, that he needs the approval, but you said that there was a concurrence that you need to go see Milosevic. "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: Well, you know, I can't remember exactly, but the conclusion was that Milosevic would have to resolve this. "MR. HARDIN: I understand that. I'm trying to understand who was involved at that time, when you came to that conclusion. "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: Well, they took me to Maksic -- "MR. HARDIN: I know, but who was there? "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: Well, Rasuo, Kalicanin, Maksic, and myself. "MR. HARDIN: That's what I asked you. Okay. "WITNESS MILAN BABIC: Well, I already mentioned it, so I thought -- "MR. HARDIN: I know, but I want to confirm, because sometimes it's not really clear. Okay. That's good."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's enough. I think it's enough. This is enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can go into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're in open session, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I will not be mentioning the witness's name. However, what we see on this tape makes it indisputable that several of them had met in a private apartment, all of them from the same area, and they agreed among themselves whom they would need, in terms of experts, to organise Territorial Defence. I therefore assume, Mr. MILAN BABIC, that it is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you explained some time ago that since one of them was an active-duty military man, you had agreed to ask for approval for him to leave the active force of the army and help you out with the Territorial Defence out there. Do you distinguish between finding volunteers who would go out to help you and asking approval for them to leave the army in order to help you out, on one hand, and appointing your own commanders, either by me or by military authorities in Belgrade, on the other hand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this specific case, things went like this: They found a man who was ready to go. He was an active-duty officer. The defence administration of Belgrade, that's what he called his institution where he was employed, and he said he needed your approval to go. As for the rest of the developments, I described them as best I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How could I possibly approve for someone to leave the defence administration of Belgrade? You said even on tape that I would be supposed to ask the competent military authorities for approval for this man to be put at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approval for him to go, yes. Use your clout to make it possible for him to go, from the position that you held.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said yourself that I was supposed to ask for this man to be released from his duties.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We wanted him to be released from the army to help us organise the Territorial Defence of SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The idea seems one that pleases you, the idea of me approving every single decision of yours. Can you tell me how you made the selection and appointments of individuals in the Territorial Defence and later the Serbian army of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Simovic said that it was you who decided that it should be General Djujic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters can't hear the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned he was a retired officer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Rather than an active-duty officer. So I suppose that no one from the military authorities, and even less civilian authorities, had to approve for a retired person to go to his homeland and help out in the organisation of Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Maksic was supposed to come to this staff of Territorial Defence, with ten men, and help organise it. However, only several men came, with Colonel Kasim, and said they would make a phone call to Belgrade, and said that you had decided it should be General Djujic. Maksic also came with him, but he was not a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: These associates or colleagues of yours, whatever you called them, say that it was you who decided on your own that it should be a retired general, Ilija Djujic, who would do this job. They say that what you're saying is not correct.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is correct is what Simovic said, and then followed Djujic's appointment. And they said, the three officers who came, said they had the decision of the federal secretary for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For them to be relieved from their duties in the JNA in order to help with the technical organisation of the TO in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had approval to make up the staff of the TO of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that at that meeting you heard from one of them, the one who was the leader among them, and I can't remember his name at the moment - you know it - you say you heard him say that he can gather ten officers and take them there in order to help you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what Colonel Maksic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You met with him in his own private apartment, and as fellow countrymen, people from the same home town, you came to an agreement without consulting anyone.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Maksic said that he came from Serbia proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said he was from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our homeland is Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would both you of bear in mind the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in this private arrangement of yours, if somebody volunteered to help you, then you construe it as his having to bear some sort of responsibility or guilt?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was supposed to ask for a transfer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it logical for an active-duty officer to have to ask for approval from his superiors if he wanted to go there as a volunteer? Did he go there of his own will or did anyone force him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is logical, and that is why we asked approval from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't answer. Did he volunteer or did somebody order him to go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said they had the decision from the federal secretary for defence, Veljko Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're not answering again. Was he a volunteer? Is that how he represented himself to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He offered himself as a volunteer, but they arrived with the appropriate decision from the federal secretary for defence, Veljko Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So yes, they got approval to be released from active-duty service and help you out with the TO. Do you know that half-truths are worse than lies, Mr. Croatia-061?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Not a question. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I suppose it is not in dispute who commanded the Territorial Defence of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The TO of Krajina was commanded by the superior commands in the JNA in combat actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true that the TO of Krajina was under the command of the then president of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That Krajina did not have a president. It had a Prime Minister, who was supposed to be a civilian commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm talking about. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's how it should have been. But that's not the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what you're saying now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I believe we had cleared up that yesterday, especially in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. light of the assertions I made yesterday regarding your own role.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No point going back over evidence given earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I won't, in that case, address issues which will force us to go back into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please answer with precision: Apart from the MUP of Krajina that were appointed by the bodies of Krajina and which consisted of members from Krajina, the state security of Krajina, Krajina had its own Red Berets as well that were known as the Red Berets of Krajina; is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hadn't heard of the Red Berets of Krajina. As for the MUP and the DB in Krajina, I have spoken about that already. At the beginning of August, the government took a decision to abolish the service of state security within the territory of SAO Krajina. And as for MUP appointments and operations, I've spoken about that already as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. To abolish the state security service sounds -- gives one one impression when you put it that way and gives a completely different impression if you tell the truth, and that is that you wanted to make a distinction, to set up an organisation like those which exist in many Western countries, to rename the state security into a security agency. Wasn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The plan was to form a new agency, and it should have been under the control of the government rather than the Ministry of the Interior and the DB of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Leave the DB of Serbia. You keep making up its responsibilities over there. Is it true that you did not abolish the service but you wanted to rename it into an agency for the security of Krajina, and you took a decision to that effect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The service of state security in the territory of Krajina was abolished, and subsequently an agency was to have been formed under the control of the government, but this was not done because it was not possible under the existing circumstances, and which I've already testified about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were rather contradictory in discussing these matters, because you say that I controlled everything, that I had command over there. Then why would a parallel structure be necessary when I was in control? Please, is it true that you've made up completely this parallel structure out of fear? Is that right or not, Mr. MILAN BABIC?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the government needed to have its own intelligence agency under its control rather than under the control of the DB of Serbia. Secondly, the parallel structure was as I have described it. At the top of that structure was the DB of Serbia, and above the DB of Serbia, you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you were the person who took the decisions. You shaped life in Krajina. You appointed the ministers, you appointed the heads of state security, the Minister of Police, the Minister of Defence; the whole organisation of life. What has parallel structure got to do with it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been addressing these issues specifically. If I need to go into them again, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that all those structures that I have listed - state security, MUP, and the TO, the army of Krajina - they had a completely separate command structure in relation to Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MUP in the Krajina was under the control of the DB of Serbia. That is under your control. The army, the Serbian army in the Republic of Srpska Krajina, was under your control. One of the ways I have already described, one of the ways in which this was done. The Territorial Defence of Krajina was controlled by the JNA, that is, by you. The DB in Krajina was formed first within the SUP, the Ministry of the Interior, and then it was abolished because you controlled it. However, it continued to operate. The government did not set up its own separate service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Doesn't the following completely annul what you are just saying, and doesn't it reveal your complete separation from what you're saying? On the 20th of August, 1991, you were the creator of establishing a unified system of Territorial Defence of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. On the 20th of August, 1991, you held a government meeting of SAO Krajina. You took the decision to establish a unified system of Territorial Defence of Krajina, and you appointed as commanders of the Territorial Defence in Kordun, Milo Dakic, and for the command of the TO of Banija, Dusan Jovic. Are those your decisions? Is this true what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decisions on appointments of Jovic and Dakic I think were taken in July 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who took those decisions? You are using the passive tense. Who took those decisions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, in my capacity of Prime Minister, who also acted as Defence Minister as that position was not filled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course you are confirming that because there are documents to prove that. Did I perhaps tell you to appoint those people? Did I perhaps tell you to appoint yourself as commander of Territorial Defence? Did I tell you to take a decision? And all those decisions that you took?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovic was appointed in order to form a legal system of Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why don't you answer my question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness finish. Now, what the accused has put to you is to challenge that he told you to appoint a commander of Territorial Defence, to take a decision. Now, you can answer that in your own time and in your own way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was asked a specific question about specific people at a specific time, and I'm going to answer that in specific terms. At the end of July, or the month of August, there were quite a number of appointments, based on the regulations in force in SAO Krajina, with the aim of establishing a unified system of Territorial Defence of SAO Krajina which would be under the control of the government of SAO Krajina. At the end of September, the Main Staff of the Territorial Defence of SAO Krajina was established and the commanders were appointed in the way I have already described. There was Maksic, Djujic, and the decision of the federal secretary for National Defence that I referred to. This was the period of September and the beginning of October. It was in this way that the formation of the unified Territorial Defence was completed, but it was not placed under the command of the bodies of SAO Krajina or the government but under the competent commands of the JNA that existed within the territory of SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the point that the accused makes, essentially, is that he had no part in those decisions; that was your decision and your decision alone, and he was independent of it. Now, what is your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My exclusive decision was the appointment of Jovic and Dakic. As for the appointment of the Main Staff of the TO of SAO Krajina, the appointment of officers Vujaklija, Officer Vujaklija, but from the appointment of the commander and the Main Staff of the Territorial Defence of SAO Krajina, he had a decisive role in that respect. He decided about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand that. Who decided about appointments? Did you proclaim yourself commander of the TO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to the law on National Defence, which was implemented on the 1st of August, 1991, the Prime Minister was ex officio the commander of the Territorial Defence of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you personally were commander of the Territorial Defence of Krajina. Did I appoint you to that position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You, together with General Simovic, Veljko Kadijevic and Adzic, appointed the Main Staff of the TO and the commander Djujic, the chief of staff, Colonel Kasum, the chief of communications, Vuletic. That was your decision. I subsequently and procedurally signed that decision as far as General Djujic is concerned. So he had two appointments. He had a decision of the federal Secretary of National Defence and a confirmation of that decision of the Prime Minister of Krajina, that is, myself. So he had two appointments. But the real one came from you, and the formal one from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. As I heard for the first time not today but these past few days, the name of this General Djujic, and since you confirm that he was a retired general, and these people of yours from Krajina say that you arbitrarily appointed him to that position and that you treated him rather badly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think we're going to get much further than this. We've been around this point quite a bit. The witness has given his explanation. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the references, the decisions regarding Milan Dakic and Dusan Jovic, they were tab 117 and 118 of the Exhibit 352, and the decision in relation to Djujic, that's tab 69 of that same exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So we have the documents which show that you proclaimed yourself commander of the Territorial Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- and not only do we have the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has dealt with this. He's explained the situation. Now, there's a conflict in evidence, no doubt, or there will be or may be. We hear what you say and the fact that you challenge it but he's given his explanation and he can't do any more, and it's a waste of time going over it again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's the whole point: What this witness of yours is claiming is in complete contradiction with the documents in your possession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Look, he's not our witness. He's a Prosecution witness. Don't forget it. Secondly, you've made the point over and over again. We have it. We'll have to consider his evidence and the documents. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the problem. I would like here to establish that what he is claiming is in complete contradiction with the documents that we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And your entire explanation is that you are some sort of a cloned person, and as such you were carrying out orders from Belgrade. Is that so? Is that your explanation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that your explanation, that you actually weren't doing anything; you were just carrying out orders from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In specific cases, I'm giving a specific answer. What specific matters are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to everything. According to everything that is known in the public, you constituted the greatest opposition to the policies of Belgrade. Now you're claiming that you were working on the basis of instructions from Belgrade. How can you explain such a contradiction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm giving concrete answers to concrete questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, for instance, I've been talking about the Territorial Defence now and about your decisions that you claim were mine. I never even heard of that what's-his-name, Dakic, or Jovic, or anyone else, any of the other ones. How could I have appointed them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that you appointed Dakic and Jovic. I said that you appointed the Main Staff of SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who did I appoint to the Main Staff of the TO of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going back over this point again. The witness has given his evidence about it. Perhaps -- no. We cannot waste time going over the same point over and over again. Now, we have it. We have the documentation. We have the evidence. We see the point you make. But perhaps the witness could answer this for us: What the accused is suggesting is that you were in fact an opponent of Belgrade - this is the way he puts it - and he says what you appear to be saying in your evidence is that you were taking orders from them. Now, it doesn't matter about how that's put, but that's the general point that he's making. And what he's saying is that there is a contradiction in this. Now, would you describe your position as taking orders from Belgrade? How would you describe your relationship to Belgrade and to the accused in particular?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I could summarise that in the briefest possible manner for the whole period that the question relates to would be that I was manipulated by Belgrade. Maybe that would be closest to the truth. But in specific cases, I responded with regard to political decisions, and I have described how I took those decisions under the influence of Belgrade and, personally, Slobodan Milosevic. Regarding the self-determination of the Serbs in Krajina to remain in Yugoslavia, that was under his influence. It was under the influence of his explanation that this was a just aim, a legal one, following his conviction that this decision would be protected by the Yugoslav People's Army. As for the formation of the Territorial Defence, I had the initiative that an independent Territorial Defence be formed in Krajina which would be under the command of the government or the authorities of SAO Krajina. However, that decision could not be implemented without the support and approval of Belgrade, or rather, Slobodan Milosevic - that is what I have already said - because the JNA was under his control, the officers, the logistics, and everything else. So support and assistance was needed to realise this, and he extended that aid by assisting and controlling that institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How? How? How did I establish my control?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You allowed officers to go there, to be reassigned to the TO of SAO Krajina, and you subordinated them to the appropriate commands of the JNA, that is, to yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Those were the officers which you yourself found privately as volunteers and asked that they be permitted to go to Krajina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was only one man, and he never came following an agreement because you had determined otherwise, and I had no choice in the matter, either to have a Territorial Defence staff or for that not to exist. And under the given circumstances, I thought it was better to have whatever kind of staff was available rather than none at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, a group came that you engaged yourself, and they came according to your specifications.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Just one man came, and that man did not become the commander, as we had agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you explained that that one man told you that he would bring in another ten men, and because he didn't bring the ten men, that, I assume, is a matter between you and him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you didn't permit him to become the commander. General Simovic said, and I asked him why he wasn't appointed a commander, he said that he was an alcoholic and that you yourself had appointed General Djujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Simovic could not have told you that, that he was an alcoholic. I don't know that. Perhaps Simovic might have known something along those lines, whether somebody in the army was an alcoholic or not. But that I had appointed him, Simovic could not have told you any nonsense of that kind.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simovic said, "We have decided, we have determined, that it be General Djujic," and I asked why not Maksic, and he said, "Because he's an alcoholic." And ten of them didn't turn up, just three of them, and Maksic never became the commander, which means that you said that that man would be a fourth man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How, then, do you decide that I made the decision, that I appointed these men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I went to ask you for your permission. I then called you up by telephone to ask whether the officers would be arriving. You said they would be arriving the next day. They didn't come the next day. They came five or six days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can only assume. I can't quite remember details of that kind, minor things, but I assume that you wanted the army to have those people released as volunteers and sent to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We asked that you should allow them to come, to help them --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To help them to come, you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you had the power of decision-making. You were able to decide and give orders or influence General Kadijevic or Adzic, whoever, who were those people's superiors, to allow them to come, and that was the procedure. That's why we went to see you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you know, I was not in a position to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you know, I was not able to order anything to either Kadijevic or Adzic. Now, on what grounds do you claim that I ordered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I think we have been through this enough. I have allowed you to go on asking more questions. The witness has told us his account. Now, this argument is not assisting. Move on to a new topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the results of your arbitrariness and self-will was that in Knin - and in Knin you convened all the commanders who were in the area of the western reaches of Krajina, and among them was, for example, General Ratko Mladic, he was one of them - and that you called a meeting and asked them, demanded, with all the authority that a Prime Minister had, that the northern Dalmatian Corps should be called the Dinarski Corps, as it was known in World War II, the Chetnik Corps, and that they should change their insignia and place the Chetnik insignia on their caps and that the first to stand up to this and oppose it was General Ratko Mladic himself, and said that while he was the commander --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this is no question. Now, ask a question. It's no good making assertions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that precisely as the result of your self-will, that you convened the meeting and called for the changes that I have specified?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. It's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So all this is a lie, is it? Fine.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you said is not correct. It is not correct that there were any decisions made as regards insignia and emblems, or what you were saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. I'm very satisfied with your answer when you said that what I was saying was not true, was not correct. I have enough witnesses to prove that you were not telling the truth. Now, tell me this: As you were talking about the fact that these people from what you call the parallel structures and then you're not able to mention more than three names, having said that, did they sow fear among the people, did they threaten anybody, those people that had arrived into the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who do you mean? Who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you mentioned Stanisic, Frenki, Simatovic, and you even said that there was a man from my own security service, which is also a lie. But the people who were there, you mentioned three of them, did they threaten anybody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Franko Simatovic was at the head of DB operations and the police around Lovrinac. He made an armoured -- constructed an armoured train which went into operation --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. MILAN BABIC, that's not what I'm asking. I'm not asking you about that. You say that your life had been threatened, your life was in jeopardy, and that they issued orders over there. How shall I put it? Did they threaten anybody? Did anybody threaten anybody, and if so, when and how and where? You said some people engaged in the liquidation of persons and other conjured-up things. Now, did these people threaten anybody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I described the case of when I was threatened, and that prompted me to call you up the next morning over the phone to ask you to withdraw Frenki in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when were you threatened? When did they threaten you? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was somewhere around the 8th or 9th of August, 1991, when Captain Dragan relinquished his command over his unit to Frenki, he handed it over to Frenki. After that, 15 or 20 minutes later, some people followed me and went to Golubic, followed me to Golubic, which was the leader of the TO detachment. They blocked the entrance. They followed me and they said who was to be killed. I escaped, and that night I was followed again and in the morning I phoned you up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that they had come to kill you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They -- these soldiers had received orders that somebody should be killed and they started shouting who was to be killed and they followed me. After Vidovdan, St. Vitus Day in 1992, Goran Opacic, the head of that special police unit, or band, or group of bandits as existed in Benkovac in the house of Vlajko Lezajic, he said, "I'm going to kill you now, Bishop."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What have I got to do with that? Who is this Goran Opacic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Goran Opacic was a policeman under the command of Martic, the DB, the state security, and your own command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who was Martic? Was Martic the head of the Krajina police? Was he the Minister of Internal Affairs of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Martic was the Minister of the Interior --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is Martic himself from Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Martic is from Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about this man Opacic? Is he from Krajina as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's from Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, well, is that Krajina? Is Benkovac in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It used to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this third man, the one you mentioned, Lezajic, is he from Krajina too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's from Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. So what have I got to do with your quarrels with Martic, Lezajic, Opacic, and all the rest and the threats you made to each other, or the swearing that went on between you? What's that got to do with me or Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer, and could the speakers be asked to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm stopping you both. One answer was lost, and there's a request from the interpreters for both of you to slow down, and I repeat that. There's no point giving evidence or asking questions if it can't be interpreted. So would you bear it in mind, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Fine. I don't know what wasn't interpreted because I wasn't following the transcript. Otherwise, you have very good interpreters, and I do believe that they have interpreted the substance of what was said. But let's move on back into open session now, because it's quite nonsensical to go into these fabrications and nebulous ideas in a private session; who quarreled with whom, et cetera, et cetera, who said something to somebody else in somebody else's house.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know that the citizens from the diaspora collected money during all those war years and they assisted the Serbs in Krajina. I'm sure you're aware of that. I have here just one example of that. It dates to the end of 1994, when a sum of money had been collected, and you can take a look at this list. These are people who live in America for the most part, or rather, American citizens. Some people gave 20 dollars, others gave 2.000 dollars, one person gave 500 dollars, another might have given a thousand dollars. But anyway, a sum was collected and the total was 169.417 dollars in that one assistance campaign and one sum that was raised for you. 169.417 US dollars was the sum that was collected and sent to you. Do you remember that? That was in 1994. You can take a look at this list of donors, and you'll be able to see. Some people gave 50, others gave 4.000, some gave 20, some gave 200. But there were many of them. They're not in order, alphabetical order or numerical order. There are four and a half pages of names. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that the Serbs from the diaspora did send assistance in money to Krajina, and this began as early on as 1990. First of all, this collection was made for Serb radio television in Knin, then there were other collection drives, and there was even some communication equipment that was sent into the region, but the DB of Serbia seized it at the airport in Belgrade --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you -- please, I'm not asking you about any communication devices that were dispatched. Now, this is your specialty; you're not answering the questions that I'm asking you, and we're seeing through that, Mr. MILAN BABIC. What I'm asking you is this, and I want a yes or no answer: The representatives of these citizens who collected these 169.000 dollars, 169,417 US dollars was the sum that had been collected, and these citizens claimed that they personally handed over that sum of money to you, that the money was never paid into either the budget of the municipality of the SAO of Krajina or any other institution, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never received the 169.000 dollars personally. It was never handed over to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that it was precisely because they had handed the money over to you personally that proceedings were brought against you; however, these court proceedings were closed to the public because of the post and position you held? Do you know about these legal proceedings that were taken because of the appropriation of these 169.417 US dollars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does the name Vladimir Velebit, an inspector, mean anything to you, who headed those legal proceedings and the investigation undertaken because of the fact that you had appropriated this money?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the proceedings led by this inspector named Vladimir Velebit, who conducted the embezzlement procedures was killed in Krajina in a way that was never found out how?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Great. As we're on the subject of finances, and you're talking off the bat about finances, quite incorrectly, do you happen to know the following: What were the contributions, or rather, donations, that were made by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to the budget of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina? Quite officially, official figures, public figures, and quite legally and lawfully.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact figure, but there are facts and figures about that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you have made statements here and observations as to some shady dealings. Do you know, for example, that with the budget of Krajina for 1992, the year 1992, all the social welfare and protection, health protection, education grants, et cetera, and allowances, amounted to 1.666.000 Krajina dinars, or 5 per cent of the overall total budget of the Republic of the RSK, for instance? And at the same time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One thing at a time. Let the witness deal with this question. Can you assist as to that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The largest portion of the budget for Krajina was allocated for military purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're once again answering a question that I never asked you. I'm not asking you that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you enumerated all those facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're answering a question I didn't ask you about. I know you have received your instructions and you are following the lesson you have learnt --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic, that's a totally improper comment, and you know it. It cuts no ice at all for you to make these sort of comments. Now, the question that was asked was whether --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. The question that was asked was the 5 per cent for those amounts. Can you help? If you can't help, just say so. You've told us that most went on military expenditure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The figures I know date to 1995, and the Krajina had about 30.000 pensioners, that it had several thousand health workers. You mentioned something about the health care system. That means that these were the recipients of those funds for those purposes, allocated to those purposes. Now, what the exact sum was, I can't say, I can't express it in figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Croatia MILAN BABIC, had have you read the epic Gorski Vijenac, The Mountain Wreath?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you recall the verse by Njegos, the author, which says that fear tarnishes one's face, the face of a man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know many portions and verses from The Mountain Wreath by heart.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: That a man's honour is tarnished, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've had enough of the literary excursion. Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There were not 30.000 pensioners in Krajina, Mr. MILAN BABIC. You Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. ignore that because you did not deal in public affairs. You rather paraded in uniforms and took credit that didn't belong to you. There were 50.000 pensioners in Krajina. And in your budget, you had 5 per cent of funds for all those needs. And Yugoslavia, for instance, in 1993, gave 14.8 per cent - that is, almost 15 per cent - of your budget for those purposes: Health care, education, veterans, and the disabled. We have this data.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which year did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: 1993. Veterans, health care, and other allowances, 154.249.841.991 dinars, which is 14.8 per cent of the total budget of Krajina for 1993. You even --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in the government then. If you ask me about 1994, 1995 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have no clue. These --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it is not fair to put a string of figures to a witness and then claim he has no clue, and you know it. Now, if you want to cross-examine, you must do so fairly and properly, or it will be stopped. Now, have you got some figures to put in front of him? Try and do it fairly so he has the chance to answer, instead of just reeling them off. Have you got some figures that you can put in front of him to substantiate what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May. I will not squander my time quoting all the figures, but in view of his job, or jobs, he should be aware of these figures, at least approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... now, let's move on. You can either cross-examine him properly by putting the documents in front of him and asking him about them - it's not a memory test - or we'll go on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, then, since he doesn't have a memory, he says he has a visual one, and this is easy to remember visually if you look at figures, but he doesn't know that, of course. Do you know how much aid, how many thousands of barges with oil, sugar, staple foods, medicines, and other things, trailers, came to Krajina from Serbia over all these years?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krajina could not have survived without Serbia's help. That's obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many thousands of trailers arrived to Krajina from Serbia over those years?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many thousands. All I know is that we depended on Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why are you smirking here, then, and answering questions of the lady from the opposite side related to the intercept, the intercepted conversation between Karadzic and Kertes about flour, oil, blankets? Why do you laugh and why do you say that those were code-names for weapons and ammunition?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I read it as a very mildly coded conversation, very mildly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then. What terms were then used for blankets, flour, oil, sugar, medicines, and all the other things that we sent as aid to you? If "flour" was used as a term for ammunition, what term was used to denote flour proper? Let me learn something from you if I can.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, flour was called flour. What else was mentioned in that intercept? Batteries, HDZ will be receiving batteries. It is quite clear that it is a mildly coded conversation for weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, "flour" means sometimes flour, sometimes it means weapons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I never heard about Kertes sending flour to the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There is no mention of flour transports to the HDZ in that intercept.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are references to lights out, to batteries, to other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In Yugoslavia, Vojvodina is the bread basket of the country and probably the greatest bread basket in the Balkans, and they even talk about the sending of supplies which are soon going to expire because they would be getting new ones, and most of the stuff was sent from the so-called food reserves.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because Kertes was the head of that -- I'm not aware of Kertes being involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was never head of the commodity reserves directorate.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that you were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, according to you, I was head of everything in Yugoslavia, and if anybody ran over a pedestrian in the street, it's probably my fault.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that you were Kertes's boss.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was Kertes's boss, but I was not your boss. And if I had been your boss, you would not have done what you did. And is it correct that with this assertion of Croatia in 1990 and 1991, Croatia also interrupted all payments and payment transactions towards the area populated by Serbs and that there it was practically impossible to make a payment to the screw factory which you mentioned and for which you came to me to ask for assistance? They were unable to operate; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to make one distinction here. One thing here is that the Croatian government, in spring 1991, blocked and isolated from the payment system these areas, and in 1991, the giro accounts of certain factories were blocked, were frozen. For instance, the Tvik factory had its account frozen because of a 40-million debt. Certain accounts were frozen by the Croatian government because of debts, and also in the case of some enterprises, such as Splitvica, because they were politically in bad order. And payment transactions completely ceased in May 1991, in Krajina, and Krajina was no longer able to be involved in the payment system through the Croatian SDK.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it clear to you that the Republic of Serbian Krajina, facing this problem, embarked upon creating its own payment system in order to be able to function as an economic entity? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First we started with the payments system, whereas the banking system of Krajina remained within the economic territory of your Yugoslavia, in order to survive economically. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you are too susceptible to the inertia of answering in the negative to every question of mine, even those questions which seem favourable to you. Do you know that Yugoslavia had its own system of payments transactions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As of 1992, of course. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia did have its own payment system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Payments transactions were effected through the social accountancy service, the SDK, although in other countries this is done through banks, and it was even our intention to change the system and replace the SDK by banks.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard from experts that according to plans for the reform of the SDK, the SDK was supposed to be brought under the umbrella of the National Bank of Yugoslavia. Several years were necessary for this plan to be effected. The plan was to abolish the service for payment transactions within the National Bank of Yugoslavia and hand it over to specialised services. I don't know what was the situation at the time we are talking about and at what stage the implementation of the plan was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You should refrain from incorrect assumptions. Is it true that for the purposes of enabling payments to be made to the Krajina, special accounts were opened in the SDK, in the Republic of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 16th of May, 1991, the social accountancy service of the SAO Krajina was established, and all participants in the payment system opened their accounts with that service. In fact, they had accounts before, but they were not integrated. That service was integrated with the SDK of Serbia through Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Here we come back to that claim of yours, probably because you don't understand this completely. But all accounts were run through the SDK of Krajina, whereas the processing of payment orders was done in Yugoslavia by the service with which a contract on the extension of services was signed for that purpose, because you were not able to tackle the technical aspect of the job. And this was done by branch offices in Sombor, Zemun, and Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that. This was done by branch office 6 in Belgrade, and I know that before that, enterprises from Krajina opened duplicate accounts in the branch office in Belgrade. How that technically operated, who processed payment orders, who signed them, is a matter of technique and method. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, for instance, that the Republic of Serbian Krajina set up its own payments operation service and opened branch offices in Knin, Glina, Petrinja, Vukovar, Beli Manastir? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I know. We were actively working on setting up that system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that your SDK had a contract with SDK Novi Belgrade and Sombor for the processing of those payments orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a way of integrating the system, because the system itself would mean nothing if it had not been integrated with the system of Yugoslavia. It would have been just an isolated SDK system of Krajina, and it would have been stifled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that within Krajina such a system can operate, and outside the SAO Krajina, it can operate through any payments institution or bank, be it in Belgrade, New York, Geneva, or Milan? It doesn't matter. Payments transactions are effected with entities with whom you have deals.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The financial authorities in Yugoslavia resolved this in the way which was favourable to Krajina, bypassing Croatia. It was done through the FRY SDK system. That's the reason why the SDK of Krajina was integrated with the payment system of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I just explained in which way it was integrated, but let's not waste time. Is it true that on the 14th of July, 1992, the National Bank of Krajina was set up, that the so-called Krajina dinar was introduced, that the banking system was built up and completely equipped to function, both the payment system and the banking system of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the payment system, with the banking system of Krajina, cooperated with its counterparts in Yugoslavia, exclusively on the basis of the relevant regulations.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It functioned as a component part of the unified system of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I just explained to you that it is not the way you are describing it. But since you seem to have the need to continue claiming the opposite --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We needed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's entitled -- [Previous translation continues]... You may not like it, but he's entitled to give it. Your comment is of no assistance. Now, anything else you want to ask him?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right, Mr. May; the witness has the right not to know something. But he doesn't have the right to lie. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a matter for us to determine, between what you assert and the evidence he gives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that until the budget of SAO Krajina was decided in 1992, the needs of municipalities were being met, among other things, from the production and processing of oil?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The production of oil was located in the Mirkovci municipality. Other municipalities did not have this amenity for filling their budgets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that as far as this production is concerned, it did not belong to the Mirkovci municipality; it belonged to the whole of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. You were talking about municipalities, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I had two things in mind: One were municipal budgets, and another thing was the financing of the Krajina budget from its own revenues, including revenues from oil production. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The budget was filled from turnover tax on sales of oil and oil derivatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you presented a number of false pieces of information here, including that Stanisic, Kertes, and others appropriated funds from oil revenues, I have a disclaimer from Mikelic, who claims exactly the opposite. He says as follows: "It never happened, in all the time that I was Prime Minister of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, that I, with Jovica Stanisic and Mihalj Kertes, ever had a conversation regarding the sale of oil and oil derivatives in Mirkovci, let alone having a joint venture with them for sale of oil to the refinery in Pancevo. If the witness had known about such things, such serious offences, how is it possible that he did not present them at the Assembly of Serbian Krajina --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We don't want the comments of your various correspondents. What you can put to the witness is that he is not right when he asserts there was this conversation about oil derivatives. Now, you've heard that, Witness MILAN BABIC. It's suggested that that conversation never took place, there was no joint venture. What is your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I had several reports regarding the distribution of oil derivatives, and when I spoke about that, I was referring to the situation in 1994 and 1995. I heard, before that, that control over oil sources was in the hands of Mihalj Kertes, that he had a unit of his over there. I first heard that in Ilok Slavonia, he had a unit called Red Berets --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who had a unit? Excuse me. I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him finish.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that his men also controlled Djeletovci. That is a region where oil was being pumped near Mirkovci. Secondly, after the introduction of sanctions, the imposition of sanctions, after they were published and, to be more precise, the blockade, actually, towards Republika Srpska, and similarly also towards the Republic of Srpska Krajina, the trade in oil derivatives, or rather, the transit of oil derivatives, was under the control of international observers. To avoid the control of international observers, the following was done, to bypass their control. I know very well that several times at government sessions chaired by Mikelic there was a discussion on the number of cisterns and so-called "arnjevi," which was an expression used to camouflage the tanks so that they wouldn't be spotted by planes overflying the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and to not be noticed by the observers at border crossings. And I had two reports. One report came from people in Slavonia, that oil passed partially through the woods north of Sremska Raca, upstream, along the Sava River, and the other route was these camouflaged oil trucks used country roads to reach the bridge connecting the two Racas on the Sava River, and in that way they bypassed international control. Thirdly, I think this was a conversation sometime in April 1995, in the villa in Boticevo Street, attended by several participants, among them President Milosevic, Sokolovic, Stanisic, Badza, Mikelic, and there was a discussion there about oil and this problem. At that point in time, I didn't quite understand the reasons why this was a problem. I realised it was a problem when Mikelic turned up late.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the answer be shorter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him finish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mikelic was late to the meeting, and in fear sort of, he asked, "What happened, what happened?" as if he was afraid. I didn't realise anything special had happened. There was a discussion about football. I was a fan of Partizan and he of Zvezda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you can finish that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That meeting did take place, Your Honour, in April 1995. Also, in May 1995, regarding the same subject, Stanisic and Karadzic mentioned Boro Mikelic in Bijeljina. I think I've already testified about that, and if necessary, I can repeat what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand anything, anything of what you've just said. Here is what he says: The production -- Is this true, please? That is my question to you. He says that the production of crude oil was in Djeletovci, in Mirkovci municipality, and processing was done in the oil refinery in Pancevo. After processing in Pancevo, the distribution of oil derivatives was carried out through the company Nik Mirkovci and then the derivatives were directed towards public enterprises: Nik Mirkovci, Nik Vukovar, Nik Dvor na Uni, and Nik Knin. So four public companies. Through these branch companies, the oil derivatives --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let the witness answer you. You've put a series of assertions about where the processing was done and the like of it. Now, Witness, it's put to you, first of all, the processing was done in Pancevo. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. It was pumped in Djeletovci, in two ways, using the normal technology. The processing was in Pancevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's suggested the distribution was carried out through various -- through a company Nik Mirkovci, and directed towards various public enterprises. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the territory of Krajina, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So for the needs of agriculture, industry, the army of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, and for sale at petrol stations in Krajina; is that right? Sale to the public.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the -- a certain percentage of oil derivatives, every tonne produced, processed, and then returned to Krajina, that these accounts were established at every government session regarding the needs that have just been listed, that a balance was made every month of oil derivatives at government sessions of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the territory of Krajina, yes. From regular production. I wanted to say that there was also so-called extraordinary production.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am really unable to fathom what you have just said, because it follows from this that Mikelic, who was Prime Minister at the time you are talking about, he says that the balances were made at government sessions monthly, that oil was distributed throughout Krajina for all these needs - you confirmed that - and now you are saying that there was some extraordinary production. What are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't explain it technologically, but these people from Mirkovci explained to me that regular technological procedures implies pumping oil, injecting water, to maintain the stability of the soil. But there was another way of faster pumping without injecting water, something like that. I can't be very specific about this. So in this way, there were additional quantities of oil. What I testified about was the problem between determining the quotas for Krajina and Republika Srpska, namely, the method in which certain debts were balanced out between Mikelic and Karadzic was the disappearance of oil tankers passing through the Republic of -- Republika Srpska, and this was a discussion that we had at government meetings. Certain quantities of oil derivatives designated for Srpska Krajina did not arrive in Krajina, and Mikelic explained this, that Karadzic was taking them from him as they passed through the territory of Republika Srpska. So this was one of the incidents and disagreements with Karadzic that I am aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What has that got to do with Serbia, whether Mikelic and Karadzic had a dispute over a particular oil tank? And what has Karadzic got to do if an oil tank disappeared in Republika Srpska? Are you saying that Karadzic stole an oil tank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a dispute between Stanisic and Mikelic, and this was a dispute that was discussed at your offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You really believe that the state security of Serbia would address a dispute between Mikelic and Karadzic regarding an oil cistern?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One moment. This will be the last answer and then we'll adjourn. Would you deal with that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, what was the -- our last question? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You were asked about your belief. Do you believe the state security of Serbia would address a dispute between Mikelic and Karadzic concerning an oil cistern? Now, you can give an answer to that, if you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that that is what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now. 20 minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, we have, I understand, an excerpt from the last part of the interview which was played. We'll ask the registrar to give it a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked Defence Exhibit 57B, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's also, I see on the desk, the collection, the list of the collection, 69.000 dollars, or 169.000, I forget the precise amount. Do you want this exhibited, Mr. Milosevic? Yes. Give it an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, there's no reason why it should be under seal. It can be open.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Defence Exhibit 63.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's finish the question of oil. The Ministry of Energy and the man in charge or responsible for oil was Milivoj Kricka, the Minister of Energy; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Borislav Mikelic's government, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you're talking about that period, aren't you, when you claim what you allege happened? Do you know that Milivoj Kricka, the Minister of Energy, is also saying that you're not telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Kricka, is saying, but I do know that Kricka was drilling the Adriatic oil pipeline, or the Yugoslav pipeline, as it was known, in the area of Banija or Kordun before that pipeline in 1995 was to be set in operation in order to exhaust the oil reserves that existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. So you're now accusing the Minister of Energy for drilling the pipeline.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was Mikelic's decision, and his decision, and many people agreed with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't agree, of course.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mind. It wasn't part of my responsibility. But if that was useful for Krajina, I agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. Since you have such a critical attitude towards Mikelic's government, and him personally, are you aware that over an eight-month period of this government headed by Borislav Mikelic, that you describe in this way, industrial production went up by all of 26 per cent, and agricultural production marked an increase of 35 per cent? And the results were such that material reserves went up seven times over, and employed figures increased by 23.000 workers, which, for the conditions in Krajina, was a great deal. And also, it became possible in May to start paying out salaries to employees in public service, and these salaries had been delayed also for the pensioners, members of the army, the police of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, all this thanks to a stabilisation of economic conditions as a result of the efforts invested by this government. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that the government headed by Borislav Mikelic did achieve a lot and produced positive results in terms of stabilisation of economic and overall social life in the Republic of Srpska Krajina, especially so in the second half of 1994 and the beginning of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that one of the -- that the priorities of this government headed by Mikelic was the implementation of the Zagreb Peace Agreement, signed on the 29th of November, 1994, in the embassy of Russia, in Belgrade -- in Zagreb, sorry, and signed by Admiral Rakic, who was Minister of Defence of the Republic Srpska Krajina, and General Mile Novakovic, upon authority of Milan Martic, president of the Republic of Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please repeat that? I think you mentioned a number of things just then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question was whether it is true that one of the top priorities of that government headed by Mikelic was the implementation of the Zagreb Peace Agreement, and I mentioned, and I identified the people involved.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mentioned two agreements, one from November 1994, which was an agreement with the Croatian government on the normalisation of economic relations in certain areas, which were listed specifically, that is, traffic, oil, electricity, water supply, and railway traffic. And before that, there was another agreement that you mentioned, and that was an agreement on a ceasefire, from March 1994, signed by the persons you named. I don't know exactly, but that agreement was later confirmed by the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's right. But I also assume that you will not deny that those two agreements were linked together and that that was part of the normalisation of relations: First a ceasefire, followed by the establishment of economic relations. So I'm asking you: Is it true that a negotiating team was formed to discuss economic issues with Croatia, and before those economic negotiations with Croatia and joint activities, this agreement on a ceasefire was implemented?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ceasefire agreement was complied with. There were reports of isolated incidents, but generally it was observed. Secondly, the talks on economic relations with Croatia between representatives of the government of Krajina and representatives of the Croatian government started in August, after you had approved those talks to begin in June, and those talks ended partly with the agreement in November relating to certain economic issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that those negotiations were conducted with the participation - I would call it active participation and direct involvement - of international mediators: David Owen and Thorwald Stoltenberg and their associates, such as Kai Eide and others, and that priorities were established, and those were the opening to traffic of the Belgrade-Zagreb highway, the Yugoslav oil pipeline, the long-distance electricity cables, the water supply system, and then other economic matters and projects, such as the project to set up a joint oil company, and others? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my previous answer, I said what the agreement covered, and it is true that the negotiations started also through the mediation of international mediators that you have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now: Is it true that when final agreement was reached on all matters on which economic negotiations were conducted, that you refused to go to Zagreb because it was your estimate that your rating would go down in Krajina and, to tell you the truth, among Serbs outside of Krajina as well? Was that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the agreement was signed in Knin, in the headquarters of the peace forces for Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Again you're answering a question that I did not put to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
