utterances.text: We'll go into private session to deal with this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you where the agreement was signed. I'm talking about the negotiations which were conducted and which you refused to go to because you felt your rating would go down, not only in Krajina but among Serbs in other parts - in Republika Srpska and in Serbia - if you appear there at those negotiations in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had agreed the beginning of those negotiations with Mikelic, with Sarinic and Pasalic, who participated on behalf of the Croatian government, and I took part in all those -- all the negotiations held in Knin. I didn't go to Zagreb. But commissions that had been formed for certain matters also took part in those negotiations. For the oil pipeline, for instance, electricity, water, the highway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But my question was, and you've now partially answered it, that you didn't go to Zagreb; you refused to go to Zagreb to attend those negotiations so that your rating would not go down. I didn't ask you about anything else. Is it true that the negotiations on economic relations with the mediation of Owen and Stoltenberg, economic relations between Krajina and Croatia went on for all of three months, and that you were constantly obstructing them, that they were almost completed when, at a session of the government of Republika Srpska Krajina in Vukovar, on the 18th of November, 1994, you called in question all the elements of the agreement, saying that this would mean economic dependence on Croatia, something you could not accept? Was that how it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The following was true: I took a very active part in those negotiations. I had a very clear position regarding the linking up of the economics, the energy system, the oil pipeline, the water supply system, and transportation, which were the subject of the agreement. And I defended my position publicly and emphatically, also in the Assembly and elsewhere. But I did accept the final agreement. I agreed with it. And that agreement was approved by the government, of which I was a member, and the Assembly in which there were deputies from my party. The agreement, such as it was reached at the end, I agreed with it; but during the negotiation, I sharply defended my positions and presented my views Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what were those positions that you upheld during those negotiations? Will you tell us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for example, with regard to the power system, electricity, and the network that would link up the power system in Krajina and in Croatia. That was one point. And I insisted that it could be linked up with a 110-kilowatt power, because it can be measured. The technicians explained this to me, a professional explained it to me, and they said that with that voltage, one was able to measure the current, the flow of electricity. As for the waterworks, I demanded that water supplies be determined which were from the source the Obrovac in Krajina, and the water quotas, which would be allotted to the municipalities of Benkovac and the Zadar municipality in Croatia. So I asked that this be precisely defined, because it was an area that was subject to drought very frequently, which meant that the water supply would drop off. And if we determined a quantity of water for the Zadar municipality, or Croatia, then during the drought, there would be a water shortage for Obrovac and Benkovac. So those were the details that were elaborated and I wanted the agreement to reflect those details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you did not want to have water allowed for Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, quite the contrary. I asked that the water supply system, which was common for Obrovac, Benkovac, and Zadar, should be defined. That is to say, the water quotas to be allotted to those municipalities, that the percentage be determined, or quantities of water, not only for Zadar, so that if there was a drought, Obrovac and Benkovac would suffer the aftereffects and not have enough water supply. Now Zadar took a greater part, or greater share, previously in building the water supply system and had more users, so it was logical that Zadar be allotted larger quantities of water. But of course we had to set the quotas for the other municipalities as well, Benkovac and Obrovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's not go into all these details. What I asked you was: Is it true that at the government meeting held in Vukovar on the 18th of November, you brought into question this entire agreement, and the explanation you gave was that it was your economic dependence on Croatia and that therefore it was unacceptable to you? Just say yes or no: Yes, it was; no, it wasn't. That's all I need from you, a yes or no answer. If you say that this is not true, no problem, just say it's not true. If it is indeed not true.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that I said that, but it is not true that I brought the whole agreement into question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it is true that you said that. That's all I wanted to hear from you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it was true that I had said that but that I did not obstruct the signing of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness give his explanation. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the agreement was signed, I made some very sharp criticisms of it, and one of those statements went along those lines, in that sense. And it was also broadcast by the Belgrade Novosti studio and the papers for Belgrade, and I heard at the time that Milosevic had insisted that the provincial edition be thrown into the wastepaper basket because the statement wasn't a good one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wasn't a good statement that you were toppling the relations that were so sensitive and that you were just beginning to build up; isn't that so, Mr. MILAN BABIC?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a breaking down of those relations; it was building them up on sound foundations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: First of all you said you cannot -- you could not allow being economically reliant upon Croatia and that you made a statement to that effect.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did make a statement to that effect because I wanted it particularly -- specifically defined what sectors we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You made the statement in the way that you did.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted the relations between Krajina and Croatia to be well measured.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't want it to be dependent upon Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we had a uniform water supply system, if we all relied on the same water supply system, I wanted us to know who gets what.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were against and you reiterate as your arguments the ones set out in the agreement, and the agreement was nonetheless signed. It went through despite your opposition, Mr. MILAN BABIC; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agreement was signed because I agreed to it, but I didn't attend the signing ceremony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me then, please: Is it true that what you just said here and now, that that's what you said, you made the statement, repeated it before the government, using almost the very same words, at the Assembly in Vukovar. After that, you asked for new corrections to be made, adjustments, and new formulations. And then the agreement that was adopted at the government meeting by a two thirds majority of the Assembly later on, held on the 1st of December, 1994, you refused to sign it, or rather, you refused to attend the signing of the agreement; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've said several things there. Now, would you take the questions in turn and ask me one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then. Your position, your position whereby you were adamantly against, in opposition to it. You repeated it at the Assembly meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeated my statement at the Assembly and this was conveyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You asked for new adjustments, reformulations to be introduced into the agreement, and at the Assembly and the government ruled against your position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1995, with respect to the discussions that were held with respect to Croatia's abolishing the mandate, the term of office up until then for the UN peacekeepers, the debate continued over the agreement, and it was put on ice until that political conflict had been settled. So that's another issue. And it took place later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is quite true. But once again, you're giving us half-truths and distorting the facts. When it was signed -- let's be quite specific. Is this true -- it's all right, I don't mind, you don't have to agree. If you say it's not true, I'll accept that. So is it true that when the agreement was signed, and you didn't want to go there to the signing session, and you were in fact advertising yourself in that way, so when the agreement was signed, at that time, you and your SDS Krajina party branch had decided to launch the initiative with the government and, via the Assembly, to freeze the economic agreement with Croatia at once. Was this your self-will once again coming to the fore? Because you also say in the same breath that you wanted Krajina to become a part of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness cannot possibly answer questions of this sort. Now, what is the question, put shortly?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is the question: When the agreement was signed, you and your party, the SDS of Krajina, launched an initiative and you decided to take this initiative with the government of the RSK and through the Assembly of the RSK, to freeze the economic agreement with Croatia at once. So an agreement that had just been signed to which you were opposed, you took the initiative to have it put on ice; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that this came later on, under different circumstances and for different reasons. So there was mention of Croatia suspending, or rather, not allowing the continuation of the term of office of the UN peacekeepers, and that was a reaction, this suspending of the economic agreement with Croatia. This was caused by the decision made by the Croatian government, or rather, the priority was that the relations be settled politically first, and this was provoked by Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So this wasn't ordered by Belgrade now, but it was the Croatian government that was to blame. Well, I'm happy to hear that there's something that Belgrade isn't being blamed for. So your position to freeze the agreement, you say, was a reaction to the fact that the Croatian government did not wish to extend the mandate of the UN peacekeepers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And why didn't somebody else think of that? Why did you have to be a greater Catholic than the pope? How come Mikelic didn't think of that, to freeze the agreement, or somebody else? How come you thought of the idea and you were opposed to the agreement in the first place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that I wasn't opposed to the agreement. I explained the conditions and circumstances under which the agreement was put on ice, until this other priority, political issue, had been resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That means that you spoke out against the agreement because the agreement is what would make Krajina economically dependent upon Croatia. You did not want to attend the signing ceremony when the agreement was finally signed. You asked that it be frozen. And now you tell us that you were actually in favour of the agreement. Am I understanding? Am I reading you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have spoken at length about this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no needed to go over it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you happen to remember that that same man, Mikelic, after the dramatic events that took place in Western Slavonia at an Assembly meeting of the RSK, pointed to all the failures that the state and military leadership, the omissions they had made, and indicated that the borders, 1.600 kilometres of the borders - that was the length of them - and that there was no force, no power in the world that could defend those borders? And then you yourself took urgent steps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One at a time. The witness cannot possibly answer these sort of rambling questions. Now, what's the point? It's said that Mikelic, at an Assembly, pointed to failures and omissions and said there was no power in the world that could defend the borders. Now, is that right or not? Did he say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I remember is the Assembly that took place between the 18th and 20th of May, 1995, and at that meeting, Mikelic put forward his criticisms, and they related to cutting off, closing down the motorway at Okucani. So he accused Martic and some other people of having done that, from Western Slavonia. He said that they had caused the intervention that was called Flash, Operation Flash, in Western Slavonia, because Martic and a group of men that he mentioned had in fact blocked the motorway at Okucani, the motorway which was open, according to the agreement reached with Croatia. That was what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did Mikelic reach an agreement about the opening of the motorway?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was another portion of the economic agreement with Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And you shut down the motorway. You closed it off, out of spite.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you who closed off the motorway. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, who did, if it wasn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean me personally?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You personally and the representatives of your party at whose head you stood.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have a party of my own. I don't know how many members of the SDS Krajina were in Western Slavonia. At the time, I was the Foreign Minister, and the incident over there was caused by a group of men from Okucani and the police and Martic, who had ordered the motorway to be closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That too is not true. You're just saying what suits you. But let me ask the second part of my question. Is it true and correct that at that time you took urgent measures to put on the agenda of the Assembly in Borovo Selo the decision on the unification of the RSK with the Republika Srpska? Is that right? Is that true? Just say yes or no. Don't answer questions that I'm not asking you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't urgent procedure. It was placed on the agenda by the request of the bishop of the Serbian Orthodox Church and at the request of Karadzic, Krajisnik, Jovica Stanisic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't put it on the agenda?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did so at the initiative and following requests from three bishops of the Serbian Orthodox Church who arrived on the 16th of May in Knin, and they represented the Sabor Assembly of the Serbian Orthodox Church, which was meeting in Belgrade at the time to ask for the unification of the RSK and the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that at the time you agreed to be head of the board for the elaboration of the new constitution of the new state of the RSK and Republika Srpska, although you knew full well that a step of this kind was categorically opposed by officials in Belgrade and I personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accepted to be a member of the committee working on the issue for political reasons, which I can explain to you here if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know, are you aware, of how far we were opposed, how categorically we were opposed to completely -- a step that was not well thought out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard this from others, not from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And all the rest that you have told us about you heard from me; is that right? Fine. So everything you heard from others can be eliminated.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krajisnik and Karadzic said that at that point in time, you would not give permission for that, although that should be done. They said that should be done first and then see later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true and correct that, as to this urgent unification of the RSK and the Republika Srpska, nothing came of that? And to pull the wool over the public's eyes and the Serbs in Croatia, you drew up some initial premises of a state in common, a future state in common, together with Biljana Plavsic, the two of you did, you on behalf of the RSK and she on behalf of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radovan Karadzic, at the meeting in Bijeljina, that is to say the second meeting held on the territory of Republika Srpska, where this issue was discussed, said that now was not the time, although he insisted, he had insisted beforehand, that this be put into effect as soon as possible. Mrs. Plavsic, at that time meeting in Bijeljina, said, "Well, we have crossed ourselves so many times, made the sign of the cross for the unification of our two countries, and we can't implement it now?" What this was all about was the following: Krajisnik and Plavsic, the plan on unification, was used by them. They used the plan as a form of threat in order to further their own political ends within Bosnia-Herzegovina, or rather, as Nikola Koljevic said, in very precise terms -- Nikola Koljevic himself was on the committee working on the unification plan in Banja Luka, and he said it's following. He said: "Milan, this is a paradox, he said. We are entering into a unification alliance with you, whereas we are in an alliance with the Croats."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I don't think we need remain in private session, Mr., for the next part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As we're talking about the political status of Serbs in Krajina and in Republika Srpska, and so on and so forth, I think that we can state in open -- we can ask for answers in open session to some of the questions that have been raised and that relate to the declaration adopted at a Sabor Assembly held in Srb on the 25th of July, 1995. Could you give me your views about that declaration.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What kind of opinion do you want?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what sense do you want me to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you have said a lot of contradictory things. I would like to know whether you agreed with the contents of that declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Milosevic. Your comments on the evidence are of no assistance to anybody. No doubt you do it for your own purposes, but you don't assist the Court and it's not fair to the witness. Now, what is it you want to put, in concrete terms, as opposed to making some generalizations?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is not fair to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not fair to make these general and sometimes rather wild allegations that he's been contradicting himself and the like. Now, point out a contradiction. If you want to ask him about it, of course you're entitled to. But put things in concrete terms, not generalizations and not comments on the evidence, such as, "You've said a lot of contradictory things." Now, ask something concrete.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Forget, then, all the contradictory things he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My specific question is as follows: Now, when you take this declaration from Srb, do you agree with the text or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I agreed with that text.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then. What about today? You agreed at that time. Do you agree with it today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Today, political circumstances are different. We have behind us an experience full of political mistakes and failures. But in itself, the text of the declaration, in those times and under those circumstances, could have produced a good political effect had it not been for subsequent political abuses and your own insistence on a political process which you described as legal, whereas it ended up causing internecine conflicts and divisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We've already heard that. You explained, in response to one of my questions yesterday, that it was not the violent secession of certain republics that caused the war in Yugoslavia, and it was not the effect of the various political pressures from outside; it was, rather, the right to self-determination that caused the war.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was your explanation. The war was caused by you, by abusing and compromising that right to self-determination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then. Since you say that from today's point of view you would not today support this declaration again -- did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I referred to certain political processes which followed that declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'll read out to you something that you wrote at that time proceeding from universal principles, or rather, one universal principle, and that is the right of peoples to self-determination after secession, and proceeding from the existing norms in the constitution of the FRY and the Republic of Croatia, and especially in the Republic of Croatia, stating that the Republic of Croatia is also a state of the Serbian people of Croatia, and for purposes of protecting its sovereignty and freedom, the Serbian people populating today's unified territories hereby adopts and promulgates. What is there about it that is not honourable or principled? What do you see in it that is not politically correct and dishonest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that part of the text that you read?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can read out to you the entire declaration.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The right to self-determination should have been exercised within the boundaries of the republics where these peoples lived. That would have been a solution that would not have caused conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that is your current interpretation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my current opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know where it is in my notes, but I'll find it later. It is precisely peaceful solutions that the Presidency of the SFRY discussed at that time. Before I quote again to you a part of this declaration, do you know that in all constitutions of Croatia, until those changes that brought HDZ into power, that in all constitutions of Croatia, the Serbian people in Croatia were treated as an equal constituent nation? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Croats, Serbs, and Slovenes who lived in the Austro-Hungarian empire after the First World War united into one state with Serbia who was on the side of the victors in that war, the First World War, whereas Serbs, Croats, Slovenes, and other South Slavs in that area were on the side of the Austro-Hungarian empire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke before this Court about the way the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes was established. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was those Serbs who united together with Croats and Slovenes in this area, who united with Serbia, who were expelled from that state as if they hadn't existed before that state ever came into being.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was an agreement between the Serbian people there and the Croatian government, or rather, lack of agreement between them about the position of the Serbian people there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the record reflect that I said what period are we dealing with? Perhaps the witness can help us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MAY
utterances.text: Be quiet, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milosevic made a historical outline of the establishment of the first state in 1918, of the first state of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes, and the unification of those peoples from the previous territory of the Austro-Hungarian empire. That was one topic. Another topic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're dealing with 1918. No assistance to us, Mr. Milosevic. Now, move on to something up to date, if you want us to continue with this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I just mentioned in passing 1918 in a complex sentence addressed to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let us move on, then. Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, it is not in dispute that in all constitutions until 1990, until the HDZ appeared, the Serbian people were an equal, constituent people within Croatia and that Croatia was defined as the state of the Croatian people, the Serbian people, and other peoples living there. Was that true, Mr. MILAN BABIC?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. I spoke about that several times already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it's not an everyday political conflict between HDZ and Serbian representatives in 1990. It was about the abolishing of the status of the Serbian people in Krajina, a status which they had even before Croatia existed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said already, and let me repeat: Yes, it was a topic and the subject of the political conflict in 1990 between the political representatives of the Serbian people and the new Croatian authorities, that is, the HDZ. You interfered in that political conflict in the way I've already described.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What you described is not correct, but let me get back to this declaration of which you're now washing your hands. Let me read another passage from it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, to assist you, it's the declaration of Srb, and it's tab 10 of Exhibit 351.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this one further up I read out invokes the constitution of Croatia, which defines Croatia as a state belonging also to the Serbian people. And then it goes on to say in the declaration itself: "Within the borders of the state of Croatia, which is a state also of the Serbian people living in it, the Serbian people, based on its geographical, historical, cultural, and other characteristics, is a sovereign people, with all the rights making up the sovereignty of one people." What do you have against a stand like that? Is that an honourable position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, it was an honourable position that we fought for. It is still an honourable position from the point of view of the constitution and the status of the Serbian people in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A stance can be either principled or unprincipled. It cannot be principled at one time and not be principled today. I'll quote another passage: "One cannot, without the participation of the Serbian people in Croatia, choose the form of Yugoslav unity, especially in terms of secession. Peoples can secede, not states." Is that an appropriate position? Was it true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's in the declaration. It was true at the time. I said at the time there were two options: One in favour of the Yugoslav Federation, and staying within it, which was supported by you; and another option, supported by the HDZ, headed by Franjo Tudjman, and between these two options, we chose the option favoured by Serbia, and that's the sentence you just read.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether you accepted that option. If you had, it is to your credit, because the stance of Serbia at the time was that all nations and peoples are equal, that it was peoples who united using their right to self-determination into Yugoslavia. It was no fabrication of the regime. It is a historic fact contained in all the constitutions of Yugoslavia until that day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You forgot just one thing: Peoples exercise their equality and rights within the republics where they lived, whereas on the level of the SFRY, they exercised them through their republics. That's what you overlooked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't overlook anything. You simply don't know anything about it. Out of fear, you are now denouncing very principled positions that you held at the time, and I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment. It's alleged that you are acting out of fear in denouncing the principles you held at the time. You should have the opportunity of answering that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not giving up those views out of fear. I only believe that advocating such stands on the division of peoples in states was groundwork for conflict in war, and it was a premise, as it turned out, for the beginning of ethnic clashes on the territory of Yugoslavia, which brought about horrors and destruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wasn't it precisely the stand of Serbia and my own personal stand that peoples should not separate, that they should stay together, to preserve Yugoslavia instead? And I'm claiming, and was claiming at the time, that only if we preserve Yugoslavia, the Serbian people would remain within one state, because by creating that state in 1918, they began living in one state, although they populated various territories in that part of the world.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said that only that people would remain within one state, whereas self-determination was divided across republics. Parts of other republics who did not favour that sort of Yugoslavia also had the right to self-determination, and that caused the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the facts. It is senseless to repeat over and over again this lecture about Serbia and myself personally working for divisions and separation. If we had done that, Serbia would not have been the only one who remained with an unchanged ethnic composition throughout these years. We worked on the country for unity and preserving Yugoslavia. And this declaration which you are denouncing now reflects an honourable and principled position, and you degraded it by the moves you made. And I'll tell you about one move in particular: On the 28th of February, 1991, you made the decision, instead of this political approach and political solution, you made a decision on annexing SAO Krajina to the Republic of Serbia, although Belgrade, Serbia, and I myself were opposed to it. Wasn't this the way to resolve these principled issues? You approached them in a completely wrong way, which you are now trying to blame on your associates --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, you've been told before, Mr. Milosevic, that speeches are not questions, and we've had a speech which has lasted a minute and a half. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment. Witness MILAN BABIC, we've probably been over these matters to exhaustion, but if there's anything you want to say about anything which the accused has been asserting in the last minute and a half, you can; in particular, the decision of the 28th of February, 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 28th of February, 1991, the Serbian National Council and the Executive Council of SAO Krajina adopted a resolution on the separation of SAO Krajina from the Republic of Croatia. That was in reaction to a previous decision taken by the Republic of Croatia dated the 20th of February on separation from Yugoslavia, and this again was in line with the political logic or claims of Milosevic in Serbia that nations are entitled to self-determination, and this came after the showing of the film on Spegelj and a campaign from which the Serbs in Krajina realised that the government of Croatia was an enemy. And this decision was formalised on the 1st of April. And in the meantime, on the 16th of March, 1991, upon the request of Slobodan Milosevic, addressed to me personally by phone to support Yugoslavia, the Executive Council of SAO Krajina took a decision on separation from the Republic of Croatia and addressed a draft of the decision to the municipalities for adoption, and Municipal Assemblies adopted such a decision after that. So all this came later, from a provision in the declaration which Slobodan Milosevic supported and told me himself that this position was correct and that the JNA would uphold this principle of self-determination of nations or peoples. And these guarantees prompted the adoption of such decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wasn't my public policy what you said I told you by phone? This Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was on all TV stations, the newspapers, and everywhere, that we were advocating the preservation of Yugoslavia? So therefore, whether I spoke to you about it is quite unimportant. I addressed millions of people through the mediation of television, in favour of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but after that, you made a contradictory statement. After this talk to me, you said that Yugoslavia was not functioning, or something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Whether something is functioning or not, I don't know what you are alluding to now, but nowhere, in no statement of mine, no public appearance of mine, is there any other policy reflected except the policy of preserving Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That the peoples of Yugoslavia are entitled to self-determination, that the Serbian people are entitled to live one state, that they cannot live in four states, that a confederation is not a state but a federation, so you advocated that the Serb people should remain in a state that you were creating.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why are you making conclusions from my public statements and taking sentences out of context? The other side burnt its fingers too when it took out of context my speech in Kosovo Polje, and now it's being printed in some 50 countries to the shame and disgrace of this very institution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Nothing to do with this witness. It's nothing to do with this witness, Mr. Milosevic. Now, what is the point?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So was it clear that one -- that a principled position regarding the right to self-determination, and a principled position in favour of the preservation of Yugoslavia, is one thing, and that quite opposite to that is this crazy decision of yours on the unification of SAO Krajina with the Republic of Serbia? You know very well that Serbia opposed this, that I personally opposed it and said that it was crazy. How can you justify such a decision of yours by our position that Yugoslavia had to be preserved? Our support for Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your policy was to preserve Yugoslavia for the Serbian people, regardless of where they lived within the territory of Yugoslavia. That was an expression of your policies. That was what you advocated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You just said something that is quite right; to preserve Yugoslavia because it is in the best interest of all the Yugoslav peoples, and of course on condition that those peoples want that too. Otherwise, how could there be the right of peoples to self-determination if someone were to force a people to remain in a particular state?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is the gist of it. You were saying that other peoples need not remain in Yugoslavia, that is, in the state that you were building, but that the Serb people had to and that they have the right to and that they want to remain in that state, in that Yugoslavia that you were building. And you said to me on innumerable occasions that this right of the Serbian people in Croatia, that is, in SAO Krajina, would be protected by the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you are now claiming that you wanted to remain in Yugoslavia, under pressure, because I told you you had to stay there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said that that was our right and that the JNA would protect our right and that this was lawful and legal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to your relationship and my relationship with the JNA, and on the basis of these documents which have been produced here rather carelessly and which show many things that they were not intended to show. We'll come to that. The JNA was the Yugoslav army, was it not, Mr. MILAN BABIC? They were the armed forces of the SFRY. And the JNA protected all the Yugoslav peoples, not just the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How they protected them we can see from the consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But the JNA was protecting all the Yugoslav peoples and endeavouring to avoid the extremists exterminating each other, like you and the HDZ; isn't that right, Mr. MILAN BABIC?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA protected the Serbian people by causing misfortune and tragedy to the Croats and Muslims, and by compromising what the Serbs felt was their right, and that is the right to self-determination, which you said was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The JNA did not do evil to the Croats or the Muslims. It was the extremists who did evil, that you led, and which the JNA tried to appease and separate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think there's much point going on with this argument, and it's purely an argument, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it in dispute, then, just this: That Belgrade was emphatically against your decision to annex Krajina to Serbia in 1991, a decision that you took at the beginning of 1991? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 1st of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, 1st of April, 1991.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You personally were against it, and you called me up by phone that this decision should be annulled and that we should declare our support for Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you did that contrary to my emphatic position against the position of Serbia, and you are attributing this decision of yours on separation from Croatia and annexation with Serbia to our position and my policies. How can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said that it shouldn't be annexation with Serbia but that we should declare our support to Yugoslavia, which other peoples can leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that in 1991 there were a whole series of discussions among presidents of the six Yugoslav republics; once in Zagreb, once in Slovenia at the Brdjani Krajina, once in -- no, sorry, not in Zagreb -- yes, before Zagreb -- in Split, in Okrid [phoen], in Macedonia, in Sarajevo, in Belgrade, that in all these towns there were talks among the six presidents of the republics, and at all six of those talks, I advocated support for Yugoslavia? Is that well known or was that a secret?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is well known that you exclusively supported the federative set-up of Yugoslavia, because you said a confederation would not be a state. And at the beginning of June only you accepted Izetbegovic and Gligorov's proposal on some kind of a mixed entity. But essentially, you were in favour of Yugoslavia as a state. I even asked you whether Serbia and Croatia could form a confederation, and you said, "No. Let them go. I don't want them. I'll join with Greece." So you advocated a position in public that Yugoslavia could only be a federation, a model that you designed, that such a state could be composed not only of republics but also parts of peoples from other republics who wished to stay in that state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is your story about my concept.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that is what you explained to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. But if, in response to my emphatic opposition, you took a decision to secede and join with Serbia, and you're attributing that to my policies, then I can only imagine what kind of distorted descriptions you can give of other policies.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, you did not oppose secession from Croatia, but you opposed proclaiming annexation with Serbia. What we were supposed to say was that we wanted to stay in Yugoslavia. You insisted on this. And after your insistence, Krajina was constituted as a federal territory of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You yourself said that Yugoslavia needed to be supported, and now you are distorting things a little, saying we had to stay in Yugoslavia. I said to everyone, and I spoke on television and in the papers and at public rallies: Support Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The kind of Yugoslavia that you spoke about, that particular kind of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, didn't you say -- yes, it is true I advocated Yugoslavia, a federation, yes, but as a reasonable man, as a sensible man, I realised that one has to make compromises. One has to compromise. And you yourself said I accepted the initiative of Izetbegovic and Gligorov, which was in favour of a very loose federation. But that loose federation would nevertheless be a state. It wouldn't be any dis-united sum of independent states, a loose federation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time, Croatia took its decision on independence, Slovenia took a decision on independence, you had the Yugoslav People's Army deployed between Krajina and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're saying all kinds of things. I really don't know whether this is a waste of time for something that is absolutely worthless, a worthless testimony, which the documents themselves prove false. But the witness is valuable from another standpoint, as he will help to establish the participants involved in perjury. There's plenty of that here too. Let me ask you, please -- it's about a similar event -- that as a result of your arbitrariness, together with Andjelko Grahovac, from Banja Luka, on the 27th of June, 1991, you convened a joint session of the Assembly of SAO Krajina and an Assembly of the community of municipalities of Bosnian Krajina, and at that meeting you adopted a declaration on unification. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was our political initiative, launched from Knin and Banja Luka, at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see, from Knin and Banja Luka. To unite a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina and a part of Croatia, you who, as you say, from the very beginning wanted to continue living in Croatia. And that was in your heart and in your mind but not on your lips; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is an event from the 27th of June, 1991. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Was that an expression of self-will by an extremist, such as you, to unite parts of two different republics?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question is: Was that an expression of your arbitrary decisions which had disastrous effects for both peoples in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, on the 24th of June, in Banja Luka, an agreement on cooperation was signed between the government of SAO Krajina and the Executive Council of the Autonomous Region of Bosnian Krajina. After that came the proposal, and within the context of the developments at the time, for those territories, that is, SAO Krajina and the Autonomous Region of Bosnian Krajina, to unite. And this was a political proposal that was adopted and which appeared at a joint assembly meeting in Bosanski Grahovo. And both deputies of both Assemblies adopted it. However, upon the insistence of Radovan Karadzic, who that day even called up Radoslav Brdjanin, the president of the SDS for Bosnian Krajina, telling him that the deputies should annul that agreement, that such a decision could not be made, and the deputies from the Autonomous Region of Bosnian Krajina, that is, the Banja Luka region, dispersed home, and that was an expression of Karadzic's opposition. And that is why that idea, that decision, was never implemented, so it didn't have any consequences. It did not produce any consequences. What it did produce was your insistence for me to come to Belgrade to meet with Karadzic, and on that occasion, you and Radovan Karadzic told me that that political option was no-go at the time, and you told me that another political option should be advocated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are speaking about tab 46 and 47 in the binder 352, and in relation to the subject before, we were talking about the tab 35 of 352 and tab 64 of 351. So these were the documents discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's quite unbelievable with what insistence each and every cardinal and extremist activity of yours you are turning in your favour, even though all the data prove you false.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a comment from you which is not proper. Have you got any more questions? Or I'm going to bring this to an end, if there's just constant comment of this sort. Now, ask the witness a question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask, Mr. May, what kind of an expression is it? A proposal was made. It wasn't made. You were behind that proposal. You were the main protagonist of this crazy idea. It wasn't just made out of the blue. You initiated it, you organised it, and you caused chaos in Krajina, both the Bosnian and the SAO Croatian Krajina about unification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let the witness deal with the question. What's being said is that it wasn't a proposal that was made; it was your idea. Do you want to answer that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. The idea came from Borivoj Rasuo. I supported it, as did Andjelko Grahovac and the majority of deputies in both Assemblies. And I publicly advocated it and that is how it was adopted. But it was not implemented because Slobodan Milosevic called me to Belgrade to tell me, through Radovan Karadzic, there was a different plan for Bosnia, not that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this Borivoj Rasuo, your personal friend and political advisor, appears to have been the initiator of all your ideas. He appears to be your alter ego. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A second "you." That's what I was saying.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that he did have political influence over me until 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you had a background, an educational background that covers Latin, "verba volant scripta manent." Do you know what that means?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want to tell me something, tell me in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It means words fly and what is written remains. So whatever is written down is in contradiction to what you are saying today; is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is more literary comment. Let us go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very pleased, Mr. May, with your comments. I'm pleased that you're commenting on a proverb. Because if it was Mr. Nice commenting on it, it would be rather primitive, as it was last time with regard to a Serbian proverb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, since you're saying that the decision was not implemented, that I opposed it because it was crazy, that Radovan Karadzic was against it because he also thought it was crazy -- do you remember that in my presence, Radovan Karadzic told you that the Serbs and Muslims have excellent relationships, that your adventure was undermining the trust between the Serbs and Muslims and that it was inflicting enormous damage to harmony achieved in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Because after the multiparty elections they had very good cooperation. When I say "they," I'm referring to both Croats, Muslims, and Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you remember at what length he spoke about the disastrous effect of this initiative of yours on the mutual trust between Serbs and Muslims which he wanted to preserve?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You called me to come to Belgrade for him to tell me that there was a different plan for Bosnia and that now was not the time for the unification of the two Krajinas, but that we should wait for Alija Izetbegovic to make a wrong political move, and then he would settle accounts with him in the way he said. He said that he had Alija Izetbegovic in his little pocket and that he could deal with him whenever he wanted but that now was not the time. It was better to wait for him to make a wrong political move, and then he would settle accounts by chasing the Muslims into the river valleys and uniting all Serb territories in Bosnia-Herzegovina and annexing SAO Krajina to that territory. That was the plan. That's what he presented to me in your presence. And then you said, "Don't be stubborn," addressed to me, and, "Don't stand in Radovan's way." So you called me for him to announce this plan to me, which I assume you had designed together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that was going to be my next question. I was going to ask you: Was this in my presence? Did he say this in my presence? That's not true.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that is why you called me, for him to say that in your presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Both he and I, Mr. MILAN BABIC, were endeavouring to persuade you to give up that idiotic plan which was upsetting the whole of Yugoslavia, because questions had to be resolved by political means and not in such an arbitrary and unilateral manner. And never did he say in my presence that he had Izetbegovic in his little pocket and that he would force them into river valleys, and other such nonsense. These are all things that you added later on and made up. It appears you have an extraordinary ability to use half-truths. Half-truths --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm stopping this. I'm stopping this speech. Now, what's said is that you've made this up. Can you deal very briefly with it, please, Witness MILAN BABIC.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not true that I've made it up. What is true is that Slobodan Milosevic invited me to Belgrade for Radovan Karadzic to tell me, in his presence, about a plan that he agreed with, and that plan was that what we were doing in Bosnia and Grahovo could not be implemented just then and that there was another plan for Bosnia-Herzegovina, what I've already said that Radovan said. And Milosevic, after Radovan Karadzic told me this, told me not to be stubborn, not to continue insisting on my plan on the unification of two Krajinas and not to stand in Karadzic's way. And after that he asked me to settle that with the leadership of SDS in Bosnian Krajina. Radoslav Brdjanin organised the meeting in Celinac with people from Bosnian Krajina for Radovan to tell them this in my presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's now time to adjourn. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. We are still in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Then I can ask him this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you say -- let us just connect the facts that you presented yourself. You say that this decision was annulled, it had no consequences. If it produced no consequences, then why did I insist that you go together with Karadzic to the Bosnian Krajina to calm down the people whom you had mobilised in such a way, creating chaos between the Serbs and the Muslims in Bosnia? Wasn't that consequence great enough for you? Why then did you go? Why was it necessary for you to go and calm them down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the declaration was never abolished. It was never implemented, because there was a different plan in play, a plan that I spoke about, and which Karadzic explained in Celinac on the same day in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Don't repeat those political explanations to me. I'm asking you about facts and you are answering me with political explanations that you are making up yourself. I'm asking you about facts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you: Why did I insist that you go there together with him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How could he say why you did something, Mr. Milosevic? He can't begin to say that. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did I tell you to go there together with Karadzic to pacify those people, to give up that crazy idea?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You told me to go with Karadzic to Celinac to explain this to the people, why it wasn't the right time to implement this idea at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us sum up a few things, a few things that you have presented so far. One: You said that you advocated peace and life within Croatia; however, you proclaimed a state of war. That is a fact. You opposed the Vance Plan. That's another fact. You decided that Krajina would be annexed to Serbia. That's a third fact. You also made a decision on the unification of Krajina with Bosnian Krajina. Yet another fact. And I, and all the other people who opposed all these moves and acts by you, of which I enumerated only a few, we, according to you, were advocating war, we had secret plans under the banner of Yugoslavship, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you ask your questions one by one?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I enumerated the questions I have already posed and to which you've given me your answers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke in detail of all the matters you are now repeating. I gave you very precise answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How can you then explain this contradiction? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You know, Mr. Milosevic, this is all argument, in which you are trying, through the witness, to argue your case. All he can do is to answer the questions you ask, which are about facts, not arguments. It will be for us to draw the conclusions and us to decide. But there's no point going on with this witness in this frame. Now, you've got a limited amount of time -- you have a limited amount of time, so you should move on rather than trying to argue. Or perhaps it may be you might be able to finish a bit earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, the problem is that when I ask about facts, the witness answers me with some political sentences he's been coached to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I've noticed that in this book by Florence Hartmann, who is the spokesperson for this illegal Prosecutor's office, who wrote against me, and in the French translation, it says -- "Milosevic, The Diagonal of a Lunatic." That's the title of the book. It says that you made a project to unify Serbs in both republics and that I prevented this project in June 1991 and that you proclaimed the Republic of Serbian Krajina, wishing to become its president, when, in December 1991, it seemed to you that Croatia would be recognised within its boundaries. What she writes here, is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke very precisely here about this political idea of the unification of the two Krajinas, the SAO Krajina and the Bosnian Krajina, and if I didn't say it before, I'll say that I was elected president on the 19th December 1991 and submitted a proposal, an application, for the recognition of Serbian Krajina by the European community, by the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, regarding this meeting on the 1st of July, 1990, in Knin, when you gathered presidents of municipalities of Benkovac, Obrovac, Donji Lapac, Gracac, Korenica, and made the decision to establish the community of municipalities of Northern Dalmatia and Lika, was it in any way attributable to any authority in Serbia or Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about a different meeting on a different date which discussed - it was in July, 5th or 6th - it discussed constitutional amendments, or rather, drafted amendments to the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Croatia, submitted by the Presidency of the Republic of Croatia. The community of municipalities, or rather, the Assembly of Knin, made a motion for establishing a community of the municipalities of Northern Dalmatia and Lika, and all this began to be implemented in end June. On the 27th of June, the Assembly of the municipality of Knin made this decision, followed by the municipality of Lapac, Gracac, et cetera. So it was a community of these municipalities. I spoke about this and I said that I did not consult anyone in Serbia about this, this was a political initiative of mine and the Assembly of Knin, designed to improve the economic situation of that region and to affirm Knin as its seat. And later it became a pivot for exercising political rights as interpreted by the SDS and by the people who led this community of municipalities. I spoke about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So nobody in Serbia had anything to do with this; right? Let me now ask you about all these rallies, where you addressed the people, made speeches, and saying the things you said. Did anyone from Serbia put pressure on you as to what you should say at these rallies and what stands you should take, in the entire year of 1990?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I made speeches, spoke out in the press, in the media, in public.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what statements you mean specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone from Serbia tell you what you should say? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At these rallies, I advocated the programme of the SDS, then I advocated the constitution of the community of municipalities of Northern Dalmatia and Lika. I used the political vocabulary and the terminology currently applied to the Croatian government, HDZ, and the historical events. As for these events, especially the Ustasha genocide, we repeated the words that were popular in the Serbian media and television. We adopted the political vocabulary that was promoted by Serbia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked: Did anyone from Serbia tell you what you should say? That's what I asked. And instead of the answer, I heard a lengthy explanation of another sort.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I think we can return into open session. I really think that we should not be spending so much time in private sessions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the Republic of Serbian Krajina set up a state commission for war crimes and the crimes of genocide, headed by Mile Dakic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was some commission, but who dealt with these issues, I really don't know. There was something in this area. I don't really know. I believe Dakic dealt with historical issues, whereas somebody else dealt [redacted], I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about the staffing of that commission. I asked you whether Krajina formed a state commission for war crimes, headed by Mile Dakic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Dakic dealt with some historical facts, but whether it was within a state commission, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about his letter of 30th September 1994 - and I assume you should be aware of it, in light of your job - a letter addressed to the Ministry of Justice of the Republic of Serbian Krajina in Knin, to which letter there was attached a list of established perpetrators of war crimes from 1990 to 1991, and he enumerated all sorts of crimes committed against the population of Krajina, descriptions of victims and perpetrators. And do you know whether the judiciary of the Krajina instituted proceedings in a single case from that list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that document exactly. I know that there were proceedings in the judiciary against perpetrators. I have already said all I knew about this, all that I could remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Answer this now: Why are you making up that at some reception in Belgrade in December 1990, or January 1991, you heard from Dobrica Cosic that Bosnian Krajina and Serbian Krajina should unite and become the seventh Yugoslav Republic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that from academician Raskovic, who said that it was an idea of Dobrica Cosic. That was before December 1990. So it was before his departure for America, and he spoke about it after he returned from America. That's the way he spoke. Raskovic said, namely, that it was Dobrica Cosic who told him about this. Raskovic advocated this thesis about the unification of the two Krajinas at rallies in the autumn, and he even said that at the water of the Una River, the two Krajinas should be united.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you said before that it was an idea of this person whom we qualified as your alter ego. How come you are saying something totally different now? Did you make this up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are now discussing political ideas presented in autumn 1990 and the events that we discussed in closed session were from June and July 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course. June and July 1991. At one point you said that in January 1991 you heard this from Dobrica Cosic at the reception in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, why don't you take a look at your own statements? They are pretty long, so you can hardly keep check of all the untruths you've uttered. But that's your problem. Anyway, we've cleared this up. You've made it all up.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you are making speeches. You're not to comment on the witness's evidence. You can do that in due course, such comment as you want. But for the moment you're supposed to be asking questions and not making denigrating comments about the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us continue with your sincere efforts to achieve peace, and so on and so forth. Did these efforts include a speech at a rally which you held on the 20th of July, 1990, before the command of the Knin Corps, and you asked the JNA to hand over their weapons? Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think when Mr. Milosevic becomes so very specific about public appearances, I think this should be done in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know which rally you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The 20th of July, 1990.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I made a lot of statements. As for a rally in front of JNA command, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry this is a private session, because I have to ask one question that I believe, Mr. May, does not belong in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you invite at that meeting the people of Krajina to armed resistance to the Ustashas and qualify the JNA as traitors, as a traitor army, because they refused to hand over their weapons? Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember a statement of that sort. I made many sharp statements at the time to comment the events related to the ban of the referendum. When did you say it was?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was on the 20th of July, 1990.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When even, according to your own claims, you had no contact yet with anyone from Serbia. There were demonstrations before the command of the corps. You asked the JNA to hand over their weapons so that you could fight against the Ustashas. You qualified the JNA as traitors because they refused to hand over their weapons to you. You don't remember saying that? You don't remember these activities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It didn't happen at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At what time did it happen, Mr. MILAN BABIC? At what time did what I just quoted happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a rally, and the statements were not like that. They followed the announcement of the referendum on the 31st of July, 1990. After that ensued sharp political debates between the representatives of the Croatian government and the Serbian National Council, in which I was involved too, and what was at question was whether the called referendum was legitimate and legal and whether it would happen or not. The Croatian government stand was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's not waste time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were sharp statements made within those debates, but not in front of any command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what I just said you claim is not true; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any rally on the 20th of July before the command of the Knin Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I said the 20th or about the 20th, in front of the headquarters, that you called for arms -- called the JNA a traitor army because they did not want to give you any weapons to fight Ustashas, as you said. Did you never say that, not on the 20th of July, but ever, at any date around about that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that way, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In what way did you say it in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked about the polemics that were going on with the Croatian government, our discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That has nothing to do with my question, your polemics with the Croatian government. Did you speak about a peace parade held on the 1st or 2nd of May of 1991 at Lake Plitvice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about a peace march that was to have been held on the 1st of May, 1991, at the Plitvice Lakes, and about the -- I informed you about that initiative as well. You asked that it should not be called a peace march but a picnic on the 2nd of May, and on the 2nd of May we did indeed hold that but it was nonetheless a peace march. The object of the march was to show that the Plitvice Lakes national park should be set apart from Krajina, that we did not agree to it being otherwise, and that this should be publicly defined as the territory of the SAO Krajina, which means that it was in fact a political protest, a peaceful one, a peaceful political protest against the situation that was introduced into Plitvice as of the 31st of March, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. As you said that I asked that it be a picnic on the 2nd of May, do you happen to know -- are you aware of the fact that throughout Yugoslavia, for 50 years after the Second World War onwards, that is to say in socialist Yugoslavia, it was customary to hold a picnic on the 2nd of May? The 1st and 2nd of May were state holidays, national holidays. It was Labour Day holiday on the 1st of May, which meant a two-day holiday, and on the 2nd of May, people would go out to have a picnic. That was customary throughout Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you told me in April when I came to see you. You said that it was customary to have a picnic on the 2nd of May and that that's what we should do and to hold the picnic on the 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 2nd of May, when everybody in Yugoslavia was picnicking and that you should go on a picnic and give up your demonstrations but to join your fellow citizens throughout Yugoslavia and go out on a picnic. That's what it was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't go out on a picnic on the 1st of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you were a communist yourself; I don't see why you didn't adhere to that custom.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't a custom in our parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure you'll deny that, that it was a custom in due course. So you wanted to hold a peace march and in the meantime you proclaimed a state of war, isn't that so? You personally did that by your decision.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A state of war in Knin was proclaimed in the way that I have already described before this Tribunal. On the 17th of August, 1990. And the peace march, or rather, the picnic, as you wanted to call it, was held on the 2nd of May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. This peace march, was that one of your ideas as well, or did Rasuo propose that you hold it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was my idea. My idea. I don't remember that anybody else suggested it to me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
