utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. As I'm not mentioning him in the capacity of an orator, I think that we could go back into open session, Mr. May. I'm not going to mention the speaker. Because some of the issues that he touched upon I should like to discuss in open session, publicly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that Mladic and the other officers of the JNA from the 9th Corps you called dirty communists?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Komunare" is the term in Serbian, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember using that term publicly. In 1992 in the political discussions surrounding the Vance Plan, these terms -- a lot of these kinds of terms were bandied about. I'm not sure about that particular one. I don't know which circumstance you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, then: Is the reason for your conflict with Mladic the call for mobilisation immediately prior to the deblocking of the JNA barracks in Zadar, Sibenik, and Split?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then. Is it true - let me be very specific here - that you called upon the inhabitants of Knin not to respond to the call-up, not to fight in a non-Serb army but to join the Territorial Defence, which you called at the time the only pure, real, true Serb army? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not in the way that you described.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How was it, then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The call to mobilisation was a public call, and it was a government decision taken by the SAO Krajina on the basis of certain decisions pursuant to some decisions of the rump Presidency of the SFRY, in October 1991. And they were called to mobilise within the forces of the SFRY. And there was another call-up in September. There was activities to mobilise certain JNA units at the request of the competent commands of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what then? What next? Were you opposed to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am telling you what I personally took part in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that you weren't the only one who said that the JNA was a non-Serb army and that therefore people shouldn't respond to the call-up, to the mobilisation call, that there were a lot of rumours going round of that nature, even in Serbia itself, that the JNA should be disbanded and a Serb guard set up in its place and so on and so forth? Do you remember any of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first part of your question I answered in my previous answer, and it is not as you say. And what was the second part of your question? I said yes, I responded to the decisions of the Yugoslav state Presidency and the calls of the JNA commands in September and October 1991 to mobilise the citizens into units and structures of the SFRY. What was your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: About the calls for people not to respond to the mobilisation call-up into the ranks of the JNA, from those days. Do you know that that happened, that they tried to undermine the JNA from within?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I know there was quite a lot of opposition in Serbia itself to this idea on the part of individuals and groups of people and they went out onto the streets to demonstrate against the mobilisation for the JNA in September and in the autumn of 1991. That's what happened in Serbia, and that is common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you say you weren't working against this mobilisation call-up in Krajina, and your explanation was that it was a traitor army, as you said, it was not a purely Serb army, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already answered that. I don't understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you say that that's not what you actually did do.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said what we did in Krajina. I've just explained that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness and Mr. Milosevic were referring to tab 161 from Exhibit 352. It's the mobilisation call of the 26th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Let's move on from this. We've been going round in circles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: An intercept was played here, as they call it, an intercept, where I am appealing to Karadzic to stand up to that wave of opposition to the JNA, and to wield his political influence to have people respond to the call-up. Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard the transcript of your conversation with Karadzic with respect to mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, was the JNA an armed force which had the task of defending and protecting the entire territory of Yugoslavia and all the Yugoslav peoples within it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA represented the armed forces of the SFRY. That's what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And is it common knowledge that in the events that took place before it was attacked itself, and before this mass blockade of the barracks started, the killing of soldiers and all the rest of it, that it exclusively presented a buffer zone, a buffer, between the conflicting parties, the warring parties, including the area of the Republic of Srpska Krajina and other territory where clashes had taken place at that time, within that time frame? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you about what I knew as to how the JNA was deployed in the area of Krajina. It was deployed after the incident which was provoked by the police, or rather, the parallel structures, which you headed, and that was the reason why the JNA was deployed on the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, I don't want to discuss those parallel structures that you have conjured up yourself and construed, but I want to ask something about the general climate and mood, and you are trying to avoid speaking about that. So I have several questions in that regard. Is it true that with the introduction of the multiparty system into the SFRY in 1989, we saw an escalation in nationalistic, secessionist tendencies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The multiparty system in the former Yugoslavia was introduced successively in the republics. Each republic would bring its own laws to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you that. Answer my question, please. Was there a burgeoning of nationalist, secessionist tendencies, precisely within that time span?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say specifically, if -- I could give you a specific answer if you tell me what party, what republic, what time you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking for you in the situation in Croatia, for example, in 1989, as well as in 1990, that is to say, before the elections, after the elections, prior to the HDZ coming to power, after the HDZ had come into power, was there an escalation of nationalist secessionist tendencies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in 1989, that was one period of time when power and authority was in the hands of the League of Communists of Croatia, that is to say, the institutions that the League controlled. Now, do you want me to say what the policy of the League of Communists of Croatia was in 1989 or what your policy was in Croatia in that same year? I don't understand what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that I don't know my own policy in Croatia? But in 1989, yes, indeed, what I'm talking about is the wave of nationalism that swept the country. Did you happen to notice anything in Croatia in 1989 and 1990 to that effect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've spoken about that before this Tribunal. I said what I'd noticed and what things happened at that time. Do you want me to speak about each of these events individually? If so, I'm ready to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And is it true that in Croatia it was this trend, this increase of nationalism, that enabled the HDZ party, as a nationalistic group, to come to the fore, to take the head positions on the political arena, and to all intents and purposes to stand at the head of all the anti-Yugoslav forces by the same token? Was that how things were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HDZ won the elections in Croatia in April and May 1991. It won the majority vote and got a place in the Sabor, or Assembly of Croatia. It received the support of the citizens for its programme. The majority voted for that party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true -- or before we move on to this other area, one, the elections, do you remember the percentages, how many votes there were in favour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A third.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The witness said "majority."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, would you check that out? I'd like you to look up the percentages.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a majority vote. We voted in the electoral units, so it won the majority of deputies for the Sabor, or Assembly. What the exact percentage was, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's true, it did win a majority of deputies in the Assembly. It got the vote. Now, is it also true that preventing this quite obviously disputable right of the Serb people to self-determination, that this was justified in Croatia by promises that were made to the effect that a future independent state of Croatia, as it said in its programme, in its plan and programme, that it would be independent, that this was justified by promises that the state would be a democratic one, a multi-ethnic one, a multiconfessional one, multicultural? Was that -- were those the promises that were made, the main incentive and arguments for the fact that nothing -- saying that nothing would change when the Serbs were pushed out of the constitution as a constituent peoples?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a basic political issue, and the political parties of Serbs in Croatia and the Serbs clashed there on the one side with the newly established Croatian authorities on the other, and this was unleashed, as of May 1990, up until December 1990, when the new Croatian constitution was adopted. The first polemics started in that period of time, and there was a clash of political views with respect to the proposals made by the Presidency, led by Franjo Tudjman, the Croatian Presidency, about the constitutional amendments to the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Croatia. And I spoke specifically on that subject. This gave rise to resistance and political opposition on the part of the representatives of the Serb people, or rather, the parties representing the Serb people, and I made a number of speeches on that occasion, as I did in December 1990, when the new constitution was enacted and passed of the Republic of Croatia, where it was no longer stipulated that the state of Croatia was also a state of the Serb peoples living in Croatia. But that constitution mentioned the Serbs as being a national minority, which in fact meant that they did not have the right to self-determination. And this constitutional determination of this constituent peoples, as they had been up until that time, and recognises the right of peoples to self-determination, up until secession from the republic, by this new constitution, the December constitution of 1990 in Croatia, this right was rescinded. It no longer existed. It was declared null and void. And so before the constitution went through, the Serbian autonomous province of Krajina, we wanted to establish it on the basis of the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Croatia, which were in force until December 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you make it brief, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Including the amendments adopted in July 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, did we have a discussion of principle at that time too? Because those people who wanted to break away said they wanted to go into Europe, move and become part of Europe within the process of European integration, and we asked ourselves: How come we're going to be included into the process of European integration quicker if, before that, we break up what had already been integrated as a multi-ethnic and multicultural factor, the kind of Yugoslavia that -- and the Yugoslavia that was a successful model? Was that clear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm talking about our public statements made with respect to those false explanations given, that we'd reach European integration quicker if we first of all break up Yugoslavia's integration. So whose idea was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was saying that there were two dominant political options at the time as to the future of Yugoslavia. One of those options was a federal one, a federalist one, which was your own. You came out in favour of a strong federation, and the right of nations to self-determination and the right of peoples to remain within Yugoslavia. The second concept at that time was Franjo Tudjman's concept, and Slovenia's concept, according to which the republics should form a confederative alliance, or rather, to reach an agreement on the disassociation of these entities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You've already said that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the European community, I don't know what your question was specifically in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You're using a lot of time for explanations in answer to things that I'm not asking you about. Tell me, with precision: Is it true that with the victory of the HDZ at the elections in 1990, this marked the beginning of an intensified anti-Serb campaign manifested in day-to-day life as well, which Raskovic described as an aggression of consciousness? It came to expression in the streets, at workplaces, through the press, posters, and so on, and even at the administrative level, which confirmed that this was an official policy towards the Serbs because there was massive firings from the state administration, and especially the police, and even from economic enterprises. There were pogroms, unlawful arrests that their own officials are even now talking about, the disappearance of individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness must have the chance to answer questions, insofar as these are questions. They sound more like speeches. But do you agree that after the elections in 1990, there was an intensified anti-Serb campaign? That's the real point that's being made.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the policy of the HDZ, that Croatia be defined as a national state of Croats and the Serbs get the status of a national minority. And the Serb representatives interpreted this as being anti-Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the interpretations of a political view. I'm asking you what you know about the dismissals, about the arrests, about the disappearance of individuals, about killings, repression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So according to you, nobody got killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness must answer. Let him answer. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as firing is concerned, from jobs, most dismissals occurred in the state administration, and especially in the police. Then people were also dismissed from other companies, and the Serbs saw this as being directed against them. Serbs were losing jobs. The Croatian authority justified this with the fact that the economy required it, that enterprises were not profitable. As for killings, murders, in 1990, I don't -- I'm not able to remember which murders you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know anything about what was happening in Croatia in 1990?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many things were happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What I mean is, you don't know of any murders, unlawful arrests, deportations, disappearance? You know nothing about that, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember any murders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's fine. You don't know anything about the murder of Serbs in 1990 anywhere in Croatia. Tell me, then, please, since you want to stick to this political level and you don't want to go into these concrete and banal events, such as killings, that you never heard of --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you what I know. Remind me. Perhaps you know something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, you had such a killing in your own family.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in August 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You probably don't remember that either.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me about 1990?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm asking you first about 1990. Later on, I'll ask you about 1991. But your answer is very important to me about 1990, that you don't know anything.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any killings from 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that among the moves whereby such a discriminatory attitude towards the Serbian people was to be justified, and the abolition of their status, the changes in the constitution, was the census -- I have the data, but I would like to hear your interpretation. According to Croatian data, in the 1991 census, there were 581.663 inhabitants of Serb ethnicity, or 12.2 per cent. And according to Serb calculations, there were 750.000 of them, or just over that, which would mean just over 17 per cent. What is your knowledge regarding these data, and was this an instance of manipulation that I mentioned at the beginning of my question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the following: The census documents from 1991 for the area of a part of SAO Krajina were submitted to the federal statistical institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the technique.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it was not submitted to the Croatian republican institute. Secondly, it was noted that many Yugoslavs were actually Serbs. So I accept the statistics as they were, but there is also another interpretation that most of those who declared themselves to be Yugoslavs were actually Serb, and there were also some interpretations that some Serbs did not dare state their ethnicity as being Serbian. There was reference to that too in those days. That was the discussion with respect to the census.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you know nothing else about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what was happening in Krajina, and I know that the census documents were not submitted to Zagreb but to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I would say that you must have known more. For instance, regarding the referendum that you organised and in which the Serbs in Croatia participated, how many votes were counted at that referendum?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a report of the commission, so it wasn't a referendum. A legal provision was applied on the right of citizens to declare their ethnicity --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about that. I'm just asking you about the number of votes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs living in Croatia took part, but also Serbs living in Serbia and elsewhere in the world - in France or other countries - so there were about -- more than 500.000 votes cast. Those were the results filed by the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It seems to me that you should know better than I do the exact figure. As far as I can remember, I saw it only once. There were 570 something thousand votes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to me it was 530.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We'll find the exact figure. That shouldn't be a problem. Maybe your memory is not quite as good as mine, which of course is no wonder. But the number of those who cast their votes, doesn't that number seem to be much closer to the census figure? Because, as you know, only the inhabitants of age cast their vote, so the real number must have been greater.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say that it is not quite certain that the process was technically correct, and some doubts lingered as to whether people outside Krajina were not counted twice in that report. But that was just a doubt. That's as much as I know about the commission's report. However, as far as I know, the Serbian National Council accepted the commission in charge of this process and these were the data presented to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Croatia-061, are you now accusing the Serbian National Council from that period of having forged the number of people who cast their votes in the referendum, that that wasn't actually correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have taken an oath to tell the truth in this Tribunal, I'm telling you of what I know, and I'm not presenting anything but that, but my knowledge about these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And your knowledge tells you that those were actually votes by Serbs from France and other countries. I don't remember what other countries you mentioned. So not just Serbs living in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. The Serbs in Croatia, the Serbs originating from Croatia, and their descendents in Serbia, and in the diaspora, Serbs originally from Croatia. I mentioned France specifically because I know exactly that reports came in from Paris.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, for your assistance, we are talking about the report on the referendum, tab 11 of Exhibit 351, and it's actually -- mentioned 567.317 people, so about 567.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you obviously now remember better, allegedly remember better the facts now than when they actually happened, do you also remember that there was an initiative to form a Croatian Orthodox Church which existed very briefly only during the days of Pavelic's NDH, independent state of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that there was an idea to form a Croatian Orthodox Church, such as existed only during the time of Pavelic's NDH?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was talk about it as being the intention of the new Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you know nothing about that? "I know that this was said to have been the intention of the Croatian authorities." Why are you again speaking indefinitely? Who was it who was saying this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly who was saying it. I know there was a man originally from Drnis who spoke about this. He said that he intended to form such a church. I don't know with precision. I can't tell you, because I don't know exactly. I do know that such a man existed. What his religion was, whether he was an Orthodox, a Catholic, a Serbo-Croat, I don't know exactly, but I do know that he specifically spoke about it, and also there was talk about it among the Serbs, that the new Croatian authority intends to form such a church. That is as much as I know from that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have been given a quotation here of the late Jovan Raskovic, academician, and I will quote him. He says: "The Serb people feels all this as a call to history for recidivism. It spreads new apprehensions and old doubts. After all this, the Croato-Serbian relationships acquire a new aspect of paranoia. The Croatian paranoia diminishes the Ustasha genocide and the Serb is renewing the genocidal memories." Were you on good terms with Raskovic in those days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that Raskovic did speak along those lines at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you share that opinion too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I expressed my opinion in public. What you have quoted is a conglomeration of views.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Shall we move a little faster when we talk about this climate? So before the elections in 1990, long before the elections - and I'm talking about this wave of nationalism - do you remember the event of the 15th of March, 1990 - the elections took place later - that Ustasha symbols were inscribed on the Serbian Orthodox Church premises in Zagreb, the capital of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were incidents of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this was in March 1990, during a period when you say that the communists were in power in Croatia and they held the situation in control. But the communists did not control the Ustashas, certainly. And do you remember that on the 16th of March, 1990, the inhabitants of Biograd On The Sea, a small tourist town close to Zadar, who read the Belgrade press were left without it because the entire delivery of press was confiscated and thrown away, and a report to that effect appeared in the press, you could have read that, on the 17th and 18th of March, 1990.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember some incidents of that kind in Primosten, and the intolerant attitude of the locals towards tourists from Serbia. There were quite a lot of reports to that effect in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that on the 30th of August, 1990, volunteer youth units of the civil defence of Croatia - you remember that? - volunteer youth units of the civil defence of Croatia, which were joined by persons from 15 to 30 years of age, started to form in local communes and municipalities in the city of Zagreb. Such units began to be formed there on the 30th of August. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard of the formation of such volunteer units. I don't remember exactly as of which date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what did you hear about it? Did you have any knowledge about it? You just heard about it, without anything more specific?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was said that this marked the beginning of the formation of armed groups at the beginning of 1991. It was said that those groups were being armed and that in this way the HDZ was arming its members and creating its own army. That was the explanation given in January. Those were the interpretations. There was even a photograph of Branimir Glavas, from Osijek - I don't exactly remember the date - showing a pistol stuck in his belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, for example, a more large-scale event: 800 faithful and priests, on the 24th of October, in Zagreb - this is the Serbian Orthodox Church of the Holy Transfiguration - demanded protection because of increased attacks? 800 of them demanding protection in October 1990? Did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know from Metropolitan Jovan that he had to leave Zagreb, that he couldn't remain in his eparchy because of these developments. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember, then, with respect to such parallel paramilitary formations that were being formed called Tjelesni Zdrug, the Croatian National Guards Corps, the Sokola Guards, volunteer youth units that I've already mentioned, et cetera, et cetera? Do you remember all these organised formations, when they started to act, what their purpose was, and what was going on, and whether anyone was disturbed as a result of this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know when the Croatian National Guard Corps was formed as an army of the Croatian government. That took place in mid-1991, in the spring. And then there were others, as far as I know, the so-called unarmed youth organisations and the ones you mentioned. You mentioned the various names. There were rumours of that. People were talking about it. But I didn't see it personally in Krajina, where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you want to say that you know nothing about that either?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about it, and I know what -- as much as I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Do you remember that the Croatian Assembly, in 1990, passed an amendment to the Croatian constitution, abolishing the Cyrillic script?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that this unleashed great polemics, this amendment to the constitution that was adopted on the 25th of July, 1995, and that we were very much against this. And I took part in this political resistance against having amendments of this kind adopted. And I said that the Assembly, the Sabor in Srb, was organised in order to demonstrate resistance to the adoption of amendments of that kind. And at that time, we saw this as being outvoting, the majority voting over the minority in the Croatian parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, as we're on the subject of the constitution of Croatia, is it true that the Croatian authorities did not uphold any of the amendments that the Serbs favoured in the constitution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my knowledge on that score is the following: First, that Raskovic was elected to the commission for preparing the constitution, drafting the constitution of Croatia. I don't think it took part in its work, though. And secondly, that the municipalities of Northern Dalmatia and Lika sent in a draft for the statute of SAO Krajina to the Croatian authorities as a proposal for discussing the new Croatian constitution. Now, how many other amendments there were, I don't know. There were other amendments tabled by deputies from other parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you don't seem to be able to answer my question --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. What was the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The question was: Is it true that the new Croatian authorities did not introduce a single amendment tabled and proposed by the Serbs, and the main one, of course, was that the Serbs in the new constitution should retain their status of nation, as they had enjoyed in the previous constitution, but many other amendments too and that not a single one of them was adopted. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many amendments there were, but it is true that the Croatian parliament, in passing the constitution, as was popularly said, threw the Serbs out of the Croatian constitution. That is true, and we did oppose this fervently. We engaged in political debate and discussion and tabled a number of proposals, but none of that was taken into account. However, there were other possibilities open as well, which means that there were discussions about a so-called proposal for cultural autonomy, which wasn't implemented at the time, and some other models which were not put into practice either, due to the escalation of incidents and raising of political tensions and conflicts to the level of incidents and - how shall I put it? - armed provocations as well, which meant this was a parallel structure which was burgeoning in Krajina, and that contributed, by the same token, to the fact that there was not a climate of tolerance for discussing the adoption of the new Croatian constitution. I'm not amnestying, if I can put it that way, this kind of nationalism at that time and auto-centrism and the authorities that brought in the new Croatian constitution without taking into account the views of the minority, or rather, the Serb people in Croatia, which had been a constituent peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. In this series of discriminatory laws, for example, the law on basic education, primary education, was that such that it did not provide for tuition for children of Serb ethnicity? And then there was the law on education and the languages of the nations and nationalities. It provided tuition for Hungarians, Ruthenians, Armenians and all the rest, and not the Serb language in Serb schools.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This we saw as a perfidious policy on the part of the HDZ and the majority in the Croatian parliament to change the name of the language and the standard language that they called Croatian -- the literary language of Croatia, to impose it to the Serb people in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the language called up until that time? What was the name of the language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That language underwent a historical evolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In Croatia, it was known as Croato-Serbian and in Serbian it was called Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was first called Croato-Serbian, then it was later on called by an unwieldy name, a very long formulation and construction, that in Croatia -- the language that was in use was Croatian, or Serbian, so Croatian literary language, which is called either the Croatian or the Serbian language, and then that formulation was changed and altered to say that the Croatian literary language was in official use in Croatia. So this was a long period of time with different variations and adjustments of the official language, as it was defined in Croatia, and this was interpreted in different ways and it was indeed the imposition of one particular variant of the language onto the Serbs as well. So this one variation was imposed on the Serbs and it was promoted by the ruling parties in the Croatian parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. There were many other laws. We mentioned them earlier on. Now, if we place all these laws into the context of the adoption of fascist emblems and symbols of a state, of a country, abolishing the right of the constituent peoples, the Serbs, the unlawful arming of paramilitary units, arrests, killings, and similar occurrences, does that lead us to the conclusion that the Croatian authorities promoted not only nationalism in Croatia but fascism and a discriminatory approach to the Serbs in Croatia, and did this lead to a great deal of unrest? Did it upset the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was all your terminology used at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, were they facts or were they terminology? So who stirred up the people and caused disturbances with the arrests, killings, persecutions, dismissals, new laws, amendments to the constitution, and so on and so forth? Were those facts or were they fabrications on the part of the Belgrade media?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we can mention some basic facts there, three basic facts, in fact: The policy of the HDZ and the Croatian authorities, and their relationship toward the Serbs; then we have political resistance and nonacquiescence of the Serbs with those kind of changes; and third, your meddling in the conflict in such a way as to produce a greater conflict. You fanned the flames of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that anybody from Serbia provoked any incidents, and if our interference in this very unwelcome turn of events -- well, whose interference was there in 1971 and in 1941? Was it also interference on the part of the same people or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We don't need to go back then. I think we've probably finished for the day. Let me add this: Mr. Milosevic, you have six hours left, if you want it, up to six hours. Mr. Tapuskovic, we've considered your application, and we will certainly grant you up to one hour to cross-examine this witness in due course. And half an hour for the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I shall abide by your decision, of course, but I should like you to understand that all the material and documents that I have looked through and had in my hands is so extensive that I will, of course, do my best to get through it in one hour, but I do really think that we amicus should be given at least a little more time in this particular instance. I will try to do my best, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've considered your application. You've got an hour. So tailor your examination accordingly. We must let this witness go. He's been giving evidence for about ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I assume that it is more important to get to the bottom of things rather than release a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Not at the expense -- one of our duties, Mr. Tapuskovic, is to conduct a trial expeditiously, and that we must do. Now, we'll have your application in mind. We'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then, I'm not sure whether I can perform my duty. I really do have to ask myself whether to continue in this position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have one hour. Now, then, tomorrow morning, please, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
